Chapter 1 · Topic 1

Modern periodic law

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 1 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Modern periodic law: physical and chemical properties repeat periodically with atomic number. Metallic character (electropositive, basic oxides, reducing) rises down and left; non-metallic rises up and right. Periodicity repeats because valence shells repeat; blocks s/p/d/f follow the filling subshell.
Key formula(s).\[ period=shell,\;Mendeleev\,fixes \]
Key points.
  • Period number = principal quantum number of valence shell.
  • Long form fixes Mendeleev anomalies (Ar-K, Co-Ni, Te-I) by atomic number.
  • Oxides: basic (metals) to amphoteric to acidic (non-metals) across a period.
  • Valency for s/p = group number or 8 minus it.
Example 1.

Most metallic among Si, Al, P, S?

  1. Metallic character falls left to right.
  2. Al (Group 13, leftmost).

Answer: Al.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Nature of Al2O3 vs Na2O vs Cl2O7?

  1. Na2O basic, Al2O3 amphoteric, Cl2O7 strongly acidic.
  2. Basic to acidic across the period.

Answer: Basic, amphoteric, acidic.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling Al2O3 purely basic.
  • Mixing period number with group number.

Chapter 1 · Topic 2

Long form periodic table

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 2 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Long form periodic table: the long form orders by atomic number into periods, groups and s/p/d/f blocks. Metallic character (electropositive, basic oxides, reducing) rises down and left; non-metallic rises up and right. Periodicity repeats because valence shells repeat; blocks s/p/d/f follow the filling subshell.
Key formula(s).\[ Mendeleev\,fixes \],\;metallic:\,Fr > Cs > \dots > F\,(least) \]
Key points.
  • Oxides: basic (metals) to amphoteric to acidic (non-metals) across a period.
  • Valency for s/p = group number or 8 minus it.
  • Period number = principal quantum number of valence shell.
  • Long form fixes Mendeleev anomalies (Ar-K, Co-Ni, Te-I) by atomic number.
Example 1.

Most metallic among Si, Al, P, S?

  1. Metallic character falls left to right.
  2. Al (Group 13, leftmost).

Answer: Al.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Nature of Al2O3 vs Na2O vs Cl2O7?

  1. Na2O basic, Al2O3 amphoteric, Cl2O7 strongly acidic.
  2. Basic to acidic across the period.

Answer: Basic, amphoteric, acidic.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling Al2O3 purely basic.
  • Mixing period number with group number.

Chapter 1 · Topic 3

Periods and groups

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 3 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Periods and groups: period number is the valence shell while group number counts valence electrons. Metallic character (electropositive, basic oxides, reducing) rises down and left; non-metallic rises up and right. Periodicity repeats because valence shells repeat; blocks s/p/d/f follow the filling subshell.
Key formula(s).\[ group\,oxidation\,state = valence\,count,\;period=shell \]
Key points.
  • Valency for s/p = group number or 8 minus it.
  • Period number = principal quantum number of valence shell.
  • Long form fixes Mendeleev anomalies (Ar-K, Co-Ni, Te-I) by atomic number.
  • Oxides: basic (metals) to amphoteric to acidic (non-metals) across a period.
Example 1.

Most non-metallic: Si, P, S, Cl?

  1. Rises right across the period.
  2. Cl.

Answer: Cl.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Amphoteric oxides among Na2O, Al2O3, SO2?

  1. Middle-period oxide reacts both ways.
  2. Al2O3.

Answer: Al2O3.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling Al2O3 purely basic.
  • Mixing period number with group number.

Blocks of periodic table

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 4 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Blocks of periodic table: s, p, d and f blocks follow the subshell receiving the last electron. Metallic character (electropositive, basic oxides, reducing) rises down and left; non-metallic rises up and right. Periodicity repeats because valence shells repeat; blocks s/p/d/f follow the filling subshell.
Key formula(s).\[ group\,oxidation\,state = valence\,count,\;period=shell,\;Mendeleev\,fixes \]

  • Period number = principal quantum number of valence shell.
  • Long form fixes Mendeleev anomalies (Ar-K, Co-Ni, Te-I) by atomic number.
  • Oxides: basic (metals) to amphoteric to acidic (non-metals) across a period.
  • Valency for s/p = group number or 8 minus it.
Example 1.

Most metallic among Si, Al, P, S?

  1. Metallic character falls left to right.
  2. Al (Group 13, leftmost).

Answer: Al.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Nature of Al2O3 vs Na2O vs Cl2O7?

  1. Na2O basic, Al2O3 amphoteric, Cl2O7 strongly acidic.
  2. Basic to acidic across the period.

Answer: Basic, amphoteric, acidic.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling Al2O3 purely basic.

Chapter 1 · Topic 6

Atomic radius

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 6 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Atomic radius: atomic size shrinks across periods on rising Zeff and swells down groups on new shells. Atomic size falls across a period (rising Zeff) and grows down a group (new shells). Cations shrink, anions swell versus parent atoms; isoelectronic series shrink with rising Z.
Key formula(s).\[ r_{covalent} < r_{metallic},\;r_{cation} < r_{atom} < r_{anion} \]
Key points.
  • Isoelectronic order e.g. \(N^{3-} > O^{2-} > F^- > Na^+ > Mg^{2+} > Al^{3+}\).
  • d-block contraction makes Ga smaller than Al; f-block gives lanthanide contraction.
  • van der Waals radius (non-bonded contact) always exceeds covalent radius.
  • Covalent radius is half a single-bond length; metallic half the lattice neighbour distance.
Example 1.

Smallest atom: Na, Mg, Al, Si?

  1. Shrinks left to right.
  2. Si.

Answer: Si.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Largest ion: N3-, O2-, F-?

  1. Lowest Z wins isoelectronic race.
  2. N3-.

Answer: N3-.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Comparing covalent with van der Waals radii directly.
  • Forgetting cations are smaller than parent atoms.

Chapter 1 · Topic 7

Covalent radius

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 7 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Covalent radius: covalent radius is half a homonuclear single-bond length. Atomic size falls across a period (rising Zeff) and grows down a group (new shells). Cations shrink, anions swell versus parent atoms; isoelectronic series shrink with rising Z.
Key formula(s).\[ r_{covalent} < r_{metallic},\;metallic\,vs\,covalent \]
Key points.
  • d-block contraction makes Ga smaller than Al; f-block gives lanthanide contraction.
  • van der Waals radius (non-bonded contact) always exceeds covalent radius.
  • Covalent radius is half a single-bond length; metallic half the lattice neighbour distance.
  • Isoelectronic order e.g. \(N^{3-} > O^{2-} > F^- > Na^+ > Mg^{2+} > Al^{3+}\).
Example 1.

Arrange \(O^{2-}, F^-, Na^+, Mg^{2+}\) in increasing size.

  1. All are 10-electron (isoelectronic); size falls as Z rises (8, 9, 11, 12).
  2. Order: \(Mg^{2+} < Na^+ < F^- < O^{2-}\).

Answer: \(Mg^{2+} < Na^+ < F^- < O^{2-}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why is \(Ga\) smaller than \(Al\) though it sits below it?

  1. Between them ten 3d electrons shield poorly.
  2. Weak shielding raises Zeff and contracts Ga (d-block contraction).

Answer: d-block contraction from poor 3d shielding.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Comparing covalent with van der Waals radii directly.
  • Forgetting cations are smaller than parent atoms.

Chapter 1 · Topic 8

Van der Waals radius

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 8 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Van der Waals radius: van der Waals radius measures unbonded contact and always exceeds covalent radius. van der Waals radius is half the closest non-bonded approach of two atoms, always larger than the covalent radius of the same element.
Key formula(s).\[ r_{vdW} > r_{covalent},\;e.g.\,Cl:\,r_{cov}=99\,pm \]
Key points.
  • Used for interlayer and molecular-crystal contacts.
  • Noble-gas radii are van der Waals type (no bonds exist).
  • Grows down a group like other radii.
Example 1.

Why is the van der Waals radius of Cl larger than its covalent radius?

  1. Covalent = shared-pair pull brings nuclei close.
  2. vdW = unshared contact with no bond shortening.

Answer: No bond shortening in vdW contact.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which radius type describes solid argon distances?

  1. Argon makes no covalent bonds.
  2. van der Waals radius.

Answer: van der Waals.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using vdW radius for bond-length sums.

Chapter 1 · Topic 9

Ionic radius

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 9 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Ionic radius: cations shrink and anions swell relative to parent atoms. Atomic size falls across a period (rising Zeff) and grows down a group (new shells). Cations shrink, anions swell versus parent atoms; isoelectronic series shrink with rising Z.
Key formula(s).\[ r_{covalent} < r_{metallic},\;r_{cation} < r_{atom} < r_{anion},\;isoelectronic:\,r \propto 1/Z \]
Key points.
  • Isoelectronic order e.g. \(N^{3-} > O^{2-} > F^- > Na^+ > Mg^{2+} > Al^{3+}\).
  • d-block contraction makes Ga smaller than Al; f-block gives lanthanide contraction.
  • van der Waals radius (non-bonded contact) always exceeds covalent radius.
  • Covalent radius is half a single-bond length; metallic half the lattice neighbour distance.
Example 1.

Smallest atom: Na, Mg, Al, Si?

  1. Shrinks left to right.
  2. Si.

Answer: Si.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Largest ion: N3-, O2-, F-?

  1. Lowest Z wins isoelectronic race.
  2. N3-.

Answer: N3-.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Comparing covalent with van der Waals radii directly.
  • Forgetting cations are smaller than parent atoms.

Chapter 1 · Topic 10

Isoelectronic species

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 10 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Isoelectronic species: isoelectronic ions shrink strictly with rising nuclear charge. Atomic size falls across a period (rising Zeff) and grows down a group (new shells). Cations shrink, anions swell versus parent atoms; isoelectronic series shrink with rising Z.
Key formula(s).\[ isoelectronic:\,r \propto 1/Z \]
Key points.
  • d-block contraction makes Ga smaller than Al; f-block gives lanthanide contraction.
  • van der Waals radius (non-bonded contact) always exceeds covalent radius.
  • Covalent radius is half a single-bond length; metallic half the lattice neighbour distance.
  • Isoelectronic order e.g. \(N^{3-} > O^{2-} > F^- > Na^+ > Mg^{2+} > Al^{3+}\).
Example 1.

Arrange \(O^{2-}, F^-, Na^+, Mg^{2+}\) in increasing size.

  1. All are 10-electron (isoelectronic); size falls as Z rises (8, 9, 11, 12).
  2. Order: \(Mg^{2+} < Na^+ < F^- < O^{2-}\).

Answer: \(Mg^{2+} < Na^+ < F^- < O^{2-}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why is \(Ga\) smaller than \(Al\) though it sits below it?

  1. Between them ten 3d electrons shield poorly.
  2. Weak shielding raises Zeff and contracts Ga (d-block contraction).

Answer: d-block contraction from poor 3d shielding.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Comparing covalent with van der Waals radii directly.
  • Forgetting cations are smaller than parent atoms.

Chapter 1 · Topic 11

Ionisation enthalpy

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 11 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Ionisation enthalpy: ionisation energy tracks Zeff over size with core-break jumps. Ionisation enthalpy is the energy to remove one mole of gaseous electrons; it rises across periods and falls down groups, jumping after noble-gas cores and at half/full subshells.
Key formula(s).\[ IE_1 < IE_2 < IE_3,\;jumps\,at\,core\,breaks \]
Key points.
  • Successive IEs jump when the next electron comes from an inner shell (Mg: IE3 huge).
  • Anomalies: Be>B (s vs p removal), N>O (half-filled stability).
  • Down a group size wins over charge: IE falls.
  • Second IE of alkali metals is enormous (noble-gas core).
Example 1.

IE1, IE2, IE3 of X are 520, 7300, 11800 kJ/mol. Identify the group.

  1. Giant jump between IE1 and IE2 means one valence electron.
  2. Alkali metal (Group 1).

Answer: Group 1.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why is IE1(O) < IE1(N)?

  1. N has exactly half-filled 2p (extra stable).
  2. O loses a paired electron more easily.

Answer: Half-filled stability of N.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading kJ values without spotting the core-break jump.
  • Assuming IE always rises uniformly.

Chapter 1 · Topic 12

Successive ionisation enthalpy

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 12 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Successive ionisation enthalpy: successive values explode when the noble-gas core is breached. Ionisation enthalpy is the energy to remove one mole of gaseous electrons; it rises across periods and falls down groups, jumping after noble-gas cores and at half/full subshells.
Key formula(s).\[ IE_1 < IE_2 < IE_3,\;jumps\,at\,core\,breaks,\;N > O \]
Key points.
  • Anomalies: Be>B (s vs p removal), N>O (half-filled stability).
  • Down a group size wins over charge: IE falls.
  • Second IE of alkali metals is enormous (noble-gas core).
  • Successive IEs jump when the next electron comes from an inner shell (Mg: IE3 huge).
Example 1.

IE1 order: Li, Be, B, C?

  1. Rises with anomaly Be > B.
  2. Li < B < Be < C.

Answer: Li<B<Be<C.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Huge IE2 jump means which group?

  1. Core breached after first electron.
  2. Group 1.

Answer: Alkali metal.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading kJ values without spotting the core-break jump.
  • Assuming IE always rises uniformly.

Chapter 1 · Topic 13

Electron gain enthalpy

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 13 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Electron gain enthalpy: gain enthalpy peaks at Cl with N near zero. Electron gain enthalpy is the energy released adding an electron to a gaseous atom; most negative for Cl (not F, due to small-size repulsion), with N, Be, Mg near zero or positive.
Key formula(s).\[ \Delta_{eg}H:\,Cl > F > Br > I \]
Key points.
  • O < S for the same size reason as F < Cl.
  • Second electron gain is always endothermic (repulsion).
  • F loses to Cl because the compact 2p repels the incoming electron.
  • Half-filled (N) and full (Be, noble) shells resist addition.
Example 1.

Why is electron gain of Cl more exothermic than F?

  1. F 2p is tiny; electron-electron repulsion offsets nuclear pull.
  2. Cl 3p is roomier, so net release is larger.

Answer: Small-orbital repulsion in F.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which has positive electron gain enthalpy: N or P?

  1. N 2p is half-filled and compact.
  2. N resists (positive); P is slightly exothermic.

Answer: N.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Blindly ranking F first in electron gain.
  • Confusing sign (exothermic = negative).

Chapter 1 · Topic 14

Electronegativity

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 14 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Electronegativity: electronegativity pull peaks at fluorine and orders bond character. Electronegativity is an atom's pull on bond electrons: F (4.0) > O > Cl > N on Pauling scale, rising across periods and falling down groups; Mulliken averages IE and EA while Allred-Rochow uses Zeff over r-squared.
Key formula(s).\[ \chi_M=\frac{IE+EA}{2},\;\chi_{AR}\propto\frac{Z_{eff}}{r^2} \]
Key points.
  • EN difference predicts bond character: >1.7 largely ionic.
  • Noble gases are skipped (no bonds to compare).
  • Across a period EN rises with Zeff; down a group size dilutes pull.
  • Diagonal pairs (Li-Mg, Be-Al) match in EN.
Example 1.

Most ionic among NaCl, MgCl2, AlCl3 by EN reasoning?

  1. Cation EN rises Na < Mg < Al, so difference shrinks.
  2. NaCl is most ionic.

Answer: NaCl.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why do BeCl2 and AlCl3 show covalent character?

  1. Small highly-charged cations polarise Cl- (Fajan).
  2. EN gap effectively narrows.

Answer: Polarisation by small cations.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning EN to noble gases.
  • Using EN difference as the only ionic test.

Chapter 1 · Topic 18

Metallic character

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 18 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Metallic character: electropositive metallic character grows down and left. Metallic character (electropositive, basic oxides, reducing) rises down and left; non-metallic rises up and right. Periodicity repeats because valence shells repeat; blocks s/p/d/f follow the filling subshell.
Key formula(s).\[ metallic:\,Fr > Cs > \dots > F\,(least) \]
Key points.
  • Valency for s/p = group number or 8 minus it.
  • Period number = principal quantum number of valence shell.
  • Long form fixes Mendeleev anomalies (Ar-K, Co-Ni, Te-I) by atomic number.
  • Oxides: basic (metals) to amphoteric to acidic (non-metals) across a period.
Example 1.

Most non-metallic: Si, P, S, Cl?

  1. Rises right across the period.
  2. Cl.

Answer: Cl.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Amphoteric oxides among Na2O, Al2O3, SO2?

  1. Middle-period oxide reacts both ways.
  2. Al2O3.

Answer: Al2O3.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling Al2O3 purely basic.
  • Mixing period number with group number.

Chapter 1 · Topic 22

Diagonal relationship

Periodic Table & Periodic PropertiesFundamentalsTopic 22 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Periodic Table and Periodic Properties, Diagonal relationship: Li-Mg and Be-Al diagonals copy each other from matching charge density. First-period elements (small, no d-orbitals, high EN) behave oddly; diagonal pairs Li-Mg and Be-Al resemble from similar charge/radius. Penetration s>p>d>f leaves d/f shielding poor, so Slater Zeff rises and lanthanides contract.
Key formula(s).\[ Li\!-\!Mg\,habits \]
Key points.
  • Inert pair: heavy p-block keeps ns2 unshared (Pb2+, Bi3+ stable).
  • Lanthanide contraction makes Zr/Hf and Nb/Ta near-twins.
  • Li-Mg and Be-Al diagonals share carbonates, nitrides, solubility habits.
  • Slater: same-shell electrons shield 0.35 (1s: 0.30); inner shells ~0.85-1.0.
Example 1.

Using Slater rules, estimate Zeff for a 3s electron of Mg (Z=12, config 1s2 2s2p8 3s2).

  1. S = 8(1.0) + 2(0.35)... inner 1s,2s2p: 2(1.0)+8(0.85)+1(0.35) = 9.15.
  2. Zeff = 12-9.15 = 2.85.

Answer: About 2.85.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why are Zr and Hf chemically twins?

  1. Lanthanide contraction cancels the expected size jump.
  2. Nearly identical radii and chemistry.

Answer: Lanthanide contraction.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying Slater 0.35 to 1s electrons (use 0.30).
  • Blaming inert pair for light elements.

First-period elements (small, no d-orbitals, high EN) behave oddly; diagonal pairs Li-Mg and Be-Al resemble from similar charge/radius. Penetration s>p>d>f leaves d/f shielding poor, so Slater Zeff rises and lanthanides contract.
Key formula(s).\[ Z_{eff}=Z-S,\;penetration:\,s>p>d>f,\;r_{La}>r_{Lu}\,by\,\sim15\,pm,\;Li\!-\!Mg\,habits,\;0.35/0.85\,Slater \]
Key points.
  • Li-Mg and Be-Al diagonals share carbonates, nitrides, solubility habits.
  • Slater: same-shell electrons shield 0.35 (1s: 0.30); inner shells ~0.85-1.0.
  • Inert pair: heavy p-block keeps ns2 unshared (Pb2+, Bi3+ stable).
  • Lanthanide contraction makes Zr/Hf and Nb/Ta near-twins.
Example 1.

Using Slater rules, estimate Zeff for a 3s electron of Mg (Z=12, config 1s2 2s2p8 3s2).

  1. S = 8(1.0) + 2(0.35)... inner 1s,2s2p: 2(1.0)+8(0.85)+1(0.35) = 9.15.
  2. Zeff = 12-9.15 = 2.85.

Answer: About 2.85.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why are Zr and Hf chemically twins?

  1. Lanthanide contraction cancels the expected size jump.
  2. Nearly identical radii and chemistry.

Answer: Lanthanide contraction.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying Slater 0.35 to 1s electrons (use 0.30).
  • Blaming inert pair for light elements.

Chapter 2 · Topic 1

Lewis structures

Chemical Bonding & Molecular StructureFundamentalsTopic 1 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure, Lewis structures: Lewis dots complete octets around the least-electronegative centre. Lewis structures distribute valence electrons to complete octets; formal charge (valence minus assigned) picks the best skeleton, and resonance averages equivalent forms into fractional bond orders.
Key formula(s).\[ FC = V-(N+\frac{B}{2}),\;best\,form:\,min|FC|,\,negative\,on\,EN\,atom \]
Key points.
  • Octet exceptions: electron-deficient (BeCl2, BF3), expanded (PCl5, SF6), odd-electron (NO, ClO2).
  • Resonance energy stabilises benzene, carbonate, ozone beyond any single form.
  • Formal charges nearest zero win; like charges stay apart.
  • Draw skeleton = least EN atom central (H never central).
Example 1.

Formal charges in O3 (central O bonded to both, one double bond)?

  1. Central O: 6-(2+3) = +1; double-bonded O: 0; single O: -1.
  2. Sum = 0 (neutral molecule).

Answer: +1, 0, -1.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Bond order of carbonate ion?

  1. Three equivalent C-O links share one double bond over 3 positions.
  2. Order = 4/3 per bond.

Answer: 1.33.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting expanded octets need period-3+ central atoms.
  • Picking resonance forms with large charge separation.

Chapter 2 · Topic 6

Ionic bond

Chemical Bonding & Molecular StructureFundamentalsTopic 6 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure, Ionic bond: ionic bonds are Coulomb lattices, not molecules. Ionic lattices are priced by lattice enthalpy (Born-Lande: rises with charge, falls with distance) and dissected by Born-Haber cycles; Fajan rules say small/highly-charged cations and large anions push bonds covalent.
Key formula(s).\[ MgO>NaCl,\;AlCl_3\,sublimes \]
Key points.
  • Coordinate bond: one-sided sharing (NH4+, [Fe(CN)6]4-, O3 terminal).
  • High lattice U means hard, high-melting salts (MgO > NaCl).
  • Born-Haber: sublimation + IE + dissociation + EA + U = formation enthalpy.
  • Fajan order e.g. NaCl < MgCl2 < AlCl3 in covalence.
Example 1.

Highest lattice enthalpy among NaCl, MgO, CaO?

  1. Charge product: MgO and CaO are 2x2; Mg2+ is smaller than Ca2+.
  2. MgO wins.

Answer: MgO.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Arrange NaCl, MgCl2, AlCl3 by melting point.

  1. Covalent character rises with cation charge (Fajan).
  2. NaCl > MgCl2 > AlCl3 (sublimes).

Answer: NaCl highest, AlCl3 lowest.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using only size and ignoring charge products.
  • Calling coordinate bonds purely ionic.

Chapter 2 · Topic 13

Bond parameters

Chemical Bonding & Molecular StructureFundamentalsTopic 13 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure, Bond parameters: length, angle, enthalpy and order describe every bond together. Bond length shortens with higher order and smaller atoms; bond angle follows repulsion hierarchy; bond enthalpy is the homolytic price per mole; bond order (MOT: half the bonding-minus-antibonding count) sets length, energy and magnetism together.
Key formula(s).\[ length \propto \frac{1}{order},\;enthalpy \propto order \]
Key points.
  • Orders: H2 1, O2 2, N2 3, CO 3 (dative-assisted triple).
  • Fractional orders from resonance (CO3 2- : 1.33).
  • Angle shrinks as lone pairs grow (CH4 109.5 to NH3 107 to H2O 104.5).
  • Shorter bonds vibrate at higher IR frequency.
Example 1.

Bond order of O2+ and its magnetism?

  1. O2 has 12 valence... order 2; removing an antibonding electron gives 2.5.
  2. One unpaired electron: paramagnetic.

Answer: 2.5, paramagnetic.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Longest bond among N2, O2, F2?

  1. Orders 3, 2, 1 respectively.
  2. F2 (single) longest.

Answer: F2.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Counting non-bonding electrons in MOT order.
  • Assuming equal orders mean equal lengths across periods.
Back to Index
Index / Fundamentals

(JEE pattern) Longest bond among N2, O2, F2?

  1. Orders 3, 2, 1 respectively.
  2. F2 (single) longest.

Answer: F2.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Counting non-bonding electrons in MOT order.

Chapter 2 · Topic 17

Bond order

Chemical Bonding & Molecular StructureFundamentalsTopic 17 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure, Bond order: bond order half the bonding-minus-antibonding count rules length and magnetism. Bond length shortens with higher order and smaller atoms; bond angle follows repulsion hierarchy; bond enthalpy is the homolytic price per mole; bond order (MOT: half the bonding-minus-antibonding count) sets length, energy and magnetism together.
Key formula(s).\[ order=\frac{N_b-N_a}{2},\;length \propto \frac{1}{order},\;lone\,pairs\,squeeze \]
Key points.
  • Fractional orders from resonance (CO3 2- : 1.33).
  • Angle shrinks as lone pairs grow (CH4 109.5 to NH3 107 to H2O 104.5).
  • Shorter bonds vibrate at higher IR frequency.
  • Orders: H2 1, O2 2, N2 3, CO 3 (dative-assisted triple).
Example 1.

Bond order of O2+ and its magnetism?

  1. O2 has 12 valence... order 2; removing an antibonding electron gives 2.5.
  2. One unpaired electron: paramagnetic.

Answer: 2.5, paramagnetic.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Longest bond among N2, O2, F2?

  1. Orders 3, 2, 1 respectively.
  2. F2 (single) longest.

Answer: F2.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Counting non-bonding electrons in MOT order.
  • Assuming equal orders mean equal lengths across periods.

Chapter 2 · Topic 18

Dipole moment

Chemical Bonding & Molecular StructureFundamentalsTopic 18 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure, Dipole moment: dipole moment vectors add over geometry to fix polarity. Dipole moment (charge times distance, in debye) vectors add over a molecule; percent ionic character benchmarks against the fully-ionic e-d value, and net zero marks non-polar geometry.
Key formula(s).\[ \mu = q\times d,\;\%\ ionic = \frac{\mu_{obs}}{\mu_{ionic}}\times100 \]
Key points.
  • Lone pairs contribute (NH3 1.47 D vs NF3 0.24 D).
  • mu = 0 is the fastest polarity test in MCQs.
  • Symmetric geometries (CO2, BF3, CCl4, PF5) cancel to zero.
  • Charge separation grows with EN gap and bond length.
Example 1.

Dipole moment of CO2 vs SO2?

  1. CO2 is linear: vectors cancel exactly.
  2. SO2 is bent with a lone pair: net mu. So 0 vs non-zero.

Answer: CO2 zero, SO2 polar.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) HCl has mu 1.08 D, bond length 127 pm. Find percent ionic character.

  1. mu-ionic = e.d = (1.602e-19)(1.27e-10) = 2.03e-29 C m = 6.1 D.
  2. % = 1.08/6.1 x 100 = 17.7%.

Answer: About 18%.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Judging polarity from bonds alone, ignoring geometry.
  • Unit slips between debye and coulomb-metre.

Chapter 2 · Topic 20

VSEPR theory

Chemical Bonding & Molecular StructureFundamentalsTopic 20 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure, VSEPR theory: VSEPR minimises electron-domain repulsion in fixed steric shapes. VSEPR arranges electron domains to minimise repulsion (lone-lone > lone-bond > bond-bond); steric number fixes electron geometry while lone pairs carve the observed molecular shape.
Key formula(s).\[ SN = \sigma + LP,\;shapes:\,2\,linear,\,3\,trigonal,\,4\,tetrahedral,\,5\,TBP,\,6\,octahedral \]
Key points.
  • 5-domain: lone pairs sit equatorial (SF4 see-saw, ClF3 T-shape, XeF2 linear).
  • 6-domain: XeF4 square planar (2 lone pairs opposite).
  • Multiple bonds squeeze angles slightly (O=C=O stays 180).
  • AX3E is pyramidal (NH3), AX2E2 bent (H2O), AX2E linear-ish bent (SO2).
Example 1.

Shape of ClF3 vs XeF2?

  1. ClF3 T-shape (2 lone pairs); XeF2 linear (3 lone pairs).
  2. T vs linear.

Answer: T-shaped and linear.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Bond angle order CH4/NH3/H2O?

  1. Lone pairs squeeze: 109.5 > 107 > 104.5.
  2. CH4 > NH3 > H2O.

Answer: Descending with lone pairs.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reporting electron geometry instead of molecular shape.
  • Putting lone pairs axial in TBP systems.

Key formula(s).\[ shapes:\,2\,linear,\,3\,trigonal,\,4\,tetrahedral,\,5\,TBP,\,6\,octahedral \]
Key points.
  • 6-domain: XeF4 square planar (2 lone pairs opposite).
  • Multiple bonds squeeze angles slightly (O=C=O stays 180).
  • AX3E is pyramidal (NH3), AX2E2 bent (H2O), AX2E linear-ish bent (SO2).
  • 5-domain: lone pairs sit equatorial (SF4 see-saw, ClF3 T-shape, XeF2 linear).
Example 1.

Shape of SF4?

  1. S has 4 bonds + 1 lone pair: SN 5, lone pair equatorial.
  2. See-saw.

Answer: See-saw.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why is H2O bent but CO2 linear?

  1. H2O oxygen carries 2 lone pairs bending the H-O-H to 104.5.
  2. CO2 carbon has zero lone pairs: linear 180.

Answer: Lone pairs on O bend water.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.

Chapter 2 · Topic 23

Valence bond theory

Chemical Bonding & Molecular StructureFundamentalsTopic 23 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure, Valence bond theory: valence bond theory overlaps atomic orbitals into directional bonds. Hybridisation mixes s/p/d into directional orbitals: sp linear, sp2 trigonal, sp3 tetrahedral, sp3d trigonal-bipyramidal, sp3d2 octahedral; lone pairs occupy hybrids and compress angles.
Key formula(s).\[ [Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}:\,dsp^2\,square,\;[CoF_6]^{3-}:\,outer,\,4\,unpaired \]
Key points.
  • s-character shortens and strengthens bonds (sp > sp2 > sp3 in EN).
  • Hypervalent (sp3d/d2) needs period-3+ centres.
  • dsp2 square planar appears for Ni2+/Pt2+ with strong ligands.
  • Count sigma bonds + lone pairs on the central atom for the steric number.
Example 1.

Hybridisation of Be in BeCl2 vapour?

  1. 2 sigma, no lone pairs.
  2. sp linear.

Answer: sp.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) s-character order sp/sp2/sp3 and EN?

  1. 50/33/25 percent; EN follows s-character.
  2. sp most electronegative.

Answer: sp > sp2 > sp3.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Counting pi bonds in the steric number.
  • Assigning sp3d to second-period centres.

Hybridisation of S in SF6 and geometry?

  2. sp3d2, octahedral.

Chapter 2 · Topic 30

Molecular orbital theory

Chemical Bonding & Molecular StructureFundamentalsTopic 30 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure, Molecular orbital theory: molecular orbitals span whole molecules via LCAO. MOT builds orbitals by LCAO: below-14-electron diatomics order sigma-2s < pi-2p < sigma-2pz; bond order half the bonding-antibonding gap decides existence, length and magnetism.
Key formula(s).\[ CO\equiv N_2\,(BO3) \]
Key points.
  • CO is isoelectronic with N2 (BO 3).
  • He2 (BO 0) does not exist.
  • B2 (1 unpaired pair... 2 unpaired), C2 diamagnetic-ish (2 pi pairs), O2 two unpaired (paramagnetic proof).
  • Heteronuclear MOs skew toward the more EN atom.
Example 1.

Which is paramagnetic: B2, C2, N2?

  1. B2 has 2 unpaired pi electrons; C2 pairs its 4 pi electrons; N2 fully paired.
  2. B2 only.

Answer: B2.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Bond order of NO and NO+?

  1. NO (11 valence... 5 bonding over antibonding excess): BO 2.5; NO+ loses antibonding: 3.0.
  2. 2.5 and 3.0.

Answer: 2.5, 3.0.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using the wrong MO order for sub-14-electron species.
  • Forgetting heteronuclear skew.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Bond order of NO and NO+?

  1. NO (11 valence... 5 bonding over antibonding excess): BO 2.5; NO+ loses antibonding: 3.0.
  2. 2.5 and 3.0.

Answer: 2.5, 3.0.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using the wrong MO order for sub-14-electron species.
  • Forgetting heteronuclear skew.

Chapter 2 · Topic 36

MO diagrams of homonuclear molecules

Chemical Bonding & Molecular StructureFundamentalsTopic 36 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure, MO diagrams of homonuclear molecules: below-14-electron diatomics swap pi above sigma-2s ordering. MOT builds orbitals by LCAO: below-14-electron diatomics order sigma-2s < pi-2p < sigma-2pz; bond order half the bonding-antibonding gap decides existence, length and magnetism.
Key formula(s).\[ BO\le0\Rightarrow no\,molecule,\;CO\equiv N_2\,(BO3) \]
Key points.
  • CO is isoelectronic with N2 (BO 3).
  • He2 (BO 0) does not exist.
  • B2 (1 unpaired pair... 2 unpaired), C2 diamagnetic-ish (2 pi pairs), O2 two unpaired (paramagnetic proof).
  • Heteronuclear MOs skew toward the more EN atom.
Example 1.

Which is paramagnetic: B2, C2, N2?

  1. B2 has 2 unpaired pi electrons; C2 pairs its 4 pi electrons; N2 fully paired.
  2. B2 only.

Answer: B2.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Bond order of NO and NO+?

  1. NO (11 valence... 5 bonding over antibonding excess): BO 2.5; NO+ loses antibonding: 3.0.
  2. 2.5 and 3.0.

Answer: 2.5, 3.0.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using the wrong MO order for sub-14-electron species.
  • Forgetting heteronuclear skew.

Chapter 2 · Topic 38

Hydrogen bonding

Chemical Bonding & Molecular StructureFundamentalsTopic 38 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure, Hydrogen bonding: N/O/F hydrogen bridges chain molecules and lift boiling points. Hydrogen bonds (H attached to N/O/F reaching another N/O/F) boost boiling points and viscosity; intermolecular links chains together while intramolecular chelates within one molecule and lowers boiling point.
Key formula(s).\[ strength:\,H\!-\!F\cdots > H\!-\!O\cdots > H\!-\!N\cdots \]
Key points.
  • o-nitrophenol (intra) boils lower than para (inter).
  • Ice floats: H-bonded open cage is less dense.
  • Strength order follows EN of the partners.
  • H2O > HF... boiling anomaly: H2O highest from 2-donor network.
Example 1.

Why does o-nitrophenol boil lower than p-nitrophenol?

  1. Ortho chelates internally, hiding H-bond donors.
  2. Para links molecules together, needing more heat.

Answer: Intra vs inter H-bonding.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Ethanol vs dimethyl ether (same mass): which boils higher?

  1. Ethanol H-bonds intermolecularly; ether cannot.
  2. Ethanol (78 C vs -24 C).

Answer: Ethanol.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling any H-contact a hydrogen bond (needs N/O/F).
  • Mixing intra and inter boiling effects.

Chapter 2 · Topic 41

Coordinate compounds and coordinate bonding

Chemical Bonding & Molecular StructureFundamentalsTopic 41 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure, Coordinate compounds and coordinate bonding: dative links build adducts like NH4+ and metal-ammine complexes. Ionic lattices are priced by lattice enthalpy (Born-Lande: rises with charge, falls with distance) and dissected by Born-Haber cycles; Fajan rules say small/highly-charged cations and large anions push bonds covalent.
Key formula(s).\[ U \propto \frac{Z^+Z^-}{r_0},\;MgO>NaCl,\;AlCl_3\,sublimes \]
Key points.
  • Fajan order e.g. NaCl < MgCl2 < AlCl3 in covalence.
  • Coordinate bond: one-sided sharing (NH4+, [Fe(CN)6]4-, O3 terminal).
  • High lattice U means hard, high-melting salts (MgO > NaCl).
  • Born-Haber: sublimation + IE + dissociation + EA + U = formation enthalpy.
Example 1.

Highest lattice enthalpy among NaCl, MgO, CaO?

  1. Charge product: MgO and CaO are 2x2; Mg2+ is smaller than Ca2+.
  2. MgO wins.

Answer: MgO.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Arrange NaCl, MgCl2, AlCl3 by melting point.

  1. Covalent character rises with cation charge (Fajan).
  2. NaCl > MgCl2 > AlCl3 (sublimes).

Answer: NaCl highest, AlCl3 lowest.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using only size and ignoring charge products.
  • Calling coordinate bonds purely ionic.

Chapter 3 · Topic 1

Position of hydrogen in periodic table

Hydrogens & p BasicsTopic 1 of 24

Explanation

Concept. In Hydrogen, Position of hydrogen in periodic table: hydrogen tops Group 1 yet gains electrons like a halogen. Hydrogen (1s1) sits atop Group 1 yet gains like a halogen; its isotopes protium, deuterium and tritium differ only in neutrons, and nascent hydrogen reduces through high reactivity.
Key formula(s).\[ ^1H,\,^2H(D),\,^3H(T),\;H:\,1s^1\,dual \]
Key points.
  • Laboratory H2: Zn + dilute acid; industrial: Bosch (water-gas shift) and electrolysis.
  • H2 burns with a pale-blue near-invisible flame.
  • Tritium is radioactive (beta, t-half ~12.3 y).
  • D2O (heavy water) moderates neutrons and shifts kinetics (isotope effect).
Example 1.

Why does D2O have a higher boiling point than H2O?

  1. Heavier molecules vibrate slower with lower zero-point energy.
  2. Stronger effective H-bonding raises bp to 101.4 C.

Answer: Heavier isotope strengthens bonding.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Lab preparation test for H2 gas evolved?

  1. Collect over water (insoluble).
  2. Burns with a pop sound.

Answer: Pop test.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Treating isotopes as chemically very different (rates differ, equilibria barely).
  • Confusing nascent with atomic hydrogen storage.

Chapter 3 · Topic 10

Hydrides

Hydrogens & p BasicsTopic 10 of 24

Explanation

Concept. In Hydrogen, Hydrides: hydrides split saline, covalent, metallic and borane-deficient families. Hydrides split saline (s-block, H-), covalent (p-block, shared), metallic/interstitial (d-block, conducting) and borane-type electron-deficient clusters; precise (CH4) and rich (NH3, H2O) complete the electron-count trio.
Key formula(s).\[ saline:\,H^-;\;BeH_2\,polymeric;\;3c\!-\!2e\,in\,B_2H_6;\;interstitial\,conduct,\;CaH_2+H_2O\to H_2 \]
Key points.
  • BeH2 and MgH2 polymerise; AlH3 is a strong reductant.
  • Metallic hydrides (Pd-H) store hydrogen in lattices.
  • Electron-rich hydrides carry lone pairs (NH3, H2O).
  • Saline hydrides hydrolyse violently: CaH2 + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + 2H2.
Example 1.

NaH + H2O gives what gas?

  1. H- + H2O -> OH- + H2.
  2. Hydrogen.

Answer: H2.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Electron-precise hydride example?

  1. CH4 owns a full octet.
  2. Methane.

Answer: CH4.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling all metal hydrides ionic.
  • Missing polymeric nature of Be/Al hydrides.

Key formula(s).\[ saline:\,H^-;\;BeH_2\,polymeric;\;3c\!-\!2e\,in\,B_2H_6;\;interstitial\,conduct,\;CaH_2+H_2O\to H_2,\;NH_3\,lone\,pair \]
Key points.
  • Metallic hydrides (Pd-H) store hydrogen in lattices.
  • Electron-rich hydrides carry lone pairs (NH3, H2O).
  • Saline hydrides hydrolyse violently: CaH2 + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + 2H2.
  • BeH2 and MgH2 polymerise; AlH3 is a strong reductant.
Example 1.

Classify CaH2 and B2H6.

  1. CaH2: s-block saline hydride with H-.
  2. B2H6: electron-deficient with 3c-2e bridges.

Answer: Saline vs electron-deficient.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which hydride conducts electricity: NaH or TiH1.7?

  1. NaH is ionic solid (conducts only molten).
  2. TiH1.7 is interstitial-metallic: conducts.

Answer: TiH1.7.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling all metal hydrides ionic.
  • Missing polymeric nature of Be/Al hydrides.

Chapter 3 · Topic 13

Metallic hydrides

Hydrogens & p BasicsTopic 13 of 24

Explanation

Concept. In Hydrogen, Metallic hydrides: interstitial hydrides conduct and store hydrogen in lattices. Hydrides split saline (s-block, H-), covalent (p-block, shared), metallic/interstitial (d-block, conducting) and borane-type electron-deficient clusters; precise (CH4) and rich (NH3, H2O) complete the electron-count trio.
Key formula(s).\[ saline:\,H^-;\;BeH_2\,polymeric;\;3c\!-\!2e\,in\,B_2H_6;\;interstitial\,conduct,\;CaH_2+H_2O\to H_2,\;BeH_2\,polymeric,\;Pd\,stores\,H \]
Key points.
  • BeH2 and MgH2 polymerise; AlH3 is a strong reductant.
  • Metallic hydrides (Pd-H) store hydrogen in lattices.
  • Electron-rich hydrides carry lone pairs (NH3, H2O).
  • Saline hydrides hydrolyse violently: CaH2 + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + 2H2.
Example 1.

NaH + H2O gives what gas?

  1. H- + H2O -> OH- + H2.
  2. Hydrogen.

Answer: H2.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Electron-precise hydride example?

  1. CH4 owns a full octet.
  2. Methane.

Answer: CH4.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling all metal hydrides ionic.
  • Missing polymeric nature of Be/Al hydrides.

Chapter 3 · Topic 14

Electron-deficient hydrides

Hydrogens & p BasicsTopic 14 of 24

Explanation

Concept. In Hydrogen, Electron-deficient hydrides: boranes bridge with 3-centre-2-electron banana bonds. Hydrides split saline (s-block, H-), covalent (p-block, shared), metallic/interstitial (d-block, conducting) and borane-type electron-deficient clusters; precise (CH4) and rich (NH3, H2O) complete the electron-count trio.
Key formula(s).\[ saline:\,H^-;\;BeH_2\,polymeric;\;3c\!-\!2e\,in\,B_2H_6;\;interstitial\,conduct,\;CaH_2+H_2O\to H_2,\;BeH_2\,polymeric \]
Key points.
  • Metallic hydrides (Pd-H) store hydrogen in lattices.
  • Electron-rich hydrides carry lone pairs (NH3, H2O).
  • Saline hydrides hydrolyse violently: CaH2 + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + 2H2.
  • BeH2 and MgH2 polymerise; AlH3 is a strong reductant.
Example 1.

Classify CaH2 and B2H6.

  1. CaH2: s-block saline hydride with H-.
  2. B2H6: electron-deficient with 3c-2e bridges.

Answer: Saline vs electron-deficient.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which hydride conducts electricity: NaH or TiH1.7?

  1. NaH is ionic solid (conducts only molten).
  2. TiH1.7 is interstitial-metallic: conducts.

Answer: TiH1.7.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling all metal hydrides ionic.
  • Missing polymeric nature of Be/Al hydrides.

Chapter 3 · Topic 17

Water

Hydrogens & p BasicsTopic 17 of 24

Explanation

Concept. In Hydrogen, Water: bent H-bonded water anomalies start from 104.5-degree polarity. Water's bent H-bonded network gives its anomalies; H2O2 adopts a non-planar open-book (dihedral ~111 deg gas) and disproportionates while acting as oxidant in acid and reductant toward stronger oxidants.
Key formula(s).\[ volume\,strength=5.6\times N \]
Key points.
  • H2O2 oxidises Fe2+/SO3 2-; reduces MnO4-/Cl2.
  • Stored dark in waxed glass (traces of alkali catalyse decay).
  • Heavy water D2O: density 1.107, bp 101.4 C, neutron moderator.
  • Volume strength: 10-vol means 1 mL gives 10 mL O2 at STP.
Example 1.

10-volume H2O2: find its normality and molarity.

  1. 10-vol gives 10 mL O2 per mL... N = vol/5.6 = 1.786 N.
  2. M = N/2 = 0.893 M.

Answer: 1.79 N, 0.89 M.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) H2O2 turns black PbS white. Explain.

  1. H2O2 oxidises PbS to PbSO4.
  2. Black sulphide becomes white sulphate.

Answer: Oxidation to PbSO4.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using vol = 11.2 x M (correct: 5.6 x N = 11.2 x M).
  • Calling H2O2 planar.

Chapter 4 · Topic 1

General characteristics

s-Block Elementss & p BasicsTopic 1 of 28

Explanation

Concept. In s-Block Elements, General characteristics: soft low-melting electropositive metals define this block. s-block metals are soft, low-melting, strongly electropositive ns1-2 metals: crimson Li, golden Na, lilac K, brick-red Ca, apple-green Ba flames; size and reactivity grow down each group.
Key formula(s).\[ flames:\,Li\,crimson,\,Na\,golden,\,K\,lilac,\,Ca\,brick\!-\!red,\,Sr\,crimson,\,Ba\,apple\!-\!green,\;blue\,glass\,unmasks\,K \]
Key points.
  • Hydration enthalpy falls down the group; lattice also falls - solubility decides winners.
  • Be/Mg differ sharply from Ca-Sr-Ba (amphoteric BeO, max covalence 4).
  • Li/Mg flames are masked (weak); use blue glass for K through Na glare.
  • Reactivity with water: Li steady, Na dancing, K flaming, Cs explosive.
Example 1.

Confirming K+ in presence of Na+ by flame: how?

  1. Na glares golden and masks lilac K.
  2. View through cobalt-blue glass: Na blocked, K lilac visible.

Answer: Cobalt-blue glass filter.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Most vigorous with water: Li, Na or K?

  1. Reactivity rises down Group 1.
  2. K (ignites instantly).

Answer: K.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reporting Ca as apple-green (that is Ba).
  • Expecting Be to behave like Ca.

Chapter 4 · Topic 6

Ionisation enthalpy

s-Block Elementss & p BasicsTopic 6 of 28

Explanation

Concept. In s-Block Elements, Ionisation enthalpy: ionisation energy tracks Zeff over size with core-break jumps. Ionisation enthalpy is the energy to remove one mole of gaseous electrons; it rises across periods and falls down groups, jumping after noble-gas cores and at half/full subshells.
Key formula(s).\[ IE_1 < IE_2 < IE_3,\;jumps\,at\,core\,breaks \]
Key points.
  • Anomalies: Be>B (s vs p removal), N>O (half-filled stability).
  • Down a group size wins over charge: IE falls.
  • Second IE of alkali metals is enormous (noble-gas core).
  • Successive IEs jump when the next electron comes from an inner shell (Mg: IE3 huge).
Example 1.

IE1 order: Li, Be, B, C?

  1. Rises with anomaly Be > B.
  2. Li < B < Be < C.

Answer: Li<B<Be<C.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Huge IE2 jump means which group?

  1. Core breached after first electron.
  2. Group 1.

Answer: Alkali metal.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading kJ values without spotting the core-break jump.
  • Assuming IE always rises uniformly.

Chapter 4 · Topic 7

Hydration enthalpy

s-Block Elementss & p BasicsTopic 7 of 28

Explanation

Concept. In s-Block Elements, Hydration enthalpy: tiny Li+/Mg2+ hydrate hardest, holding waters of crystallisation. s-block salt trends run on ion size: hydroxides/carbonates solubility rises down Group 2 while sulphates fall; carbonates/nitrates stabilise with larger cations polarising less (Fajan in reverse).
Key formula(s).\[ Li_2CO_3\,alone\,falls,\;hydration:\,Mg>Ca \]
Key points.
  • Peroxides/superoxides need big cations: K/Rb/Cs stabilise O2 -/O2 2-.
  • Hydration energy Mg2+ > Ca2+ > Sr2+ > Ba2+ (magnesium salts hold more water).
  • Li2CO3 alone decomposes on heating (tiny Li+ polarises CO3 2-).
  • Be(OH)2 amphoteric; rest basic, strength rising down.
Example 1.

Which carbonate needs the highest decomposition temperature: Li2CO3 or BaCO3?

  1. Larger cation = less distortion = more stable.
  2. BaCO3 (Li2CO3 decomposes near 700 C).

Answer: BaCO3.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Least soluble sulphate among MgSO4, CaSO4, BaSO4?

  1. Group 2 sulphate solubility falls down.
  2. BaSO4 (used as barium meal).

Answer: BaSO4.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying carbonate trend to sulphates (opposite).
  • Forgetting Li2CO3 is the unstable exception.

Chapter 4 · Topic 9

Flame colours

s-Block Elementss & p BasicsTopic 9 of 28

Explanation

Concept. In s-Block Elements, Flame colours: volatile s-block chlorides paint flames from crimson to green. s-block metals are soft, low-melting, strongly electropositive ns1-2 metals: crimson Li, golden Na, lilac K, brick-red Ca, apple-green Ba flames; size and reactivity grow down each group.
Key formula(s).\[ flames:\,Li\,crimson,\,Na\,golden,\,K\,lilac,\,Ca\,brick\!-\!red,\,Sr\,crimson,\,Ba\,apple\!-\!green,\;Na\,dances,\,K\,flames \]
Key points.
  • Reactivity with water: Li steady, Na dancing, K flaming, Cs explosive.
  • Hydration enthalpy falls down the group; lattice also falls - solubility decides winners.
  • Be/Mg differ sharply from Ca-Sr-Ba (amphoteric BeO, max covalence 4).
  • Li/Mg flames are masked (weak); use blue glass for K through Na glare.
Example 1.

Confirming K+ in presence of Na+ by flame: how?

  1. Na glares golden and masks lilac K.
  2. View through cobalt-blue glass: Na blocked, K lilac visible.

Answer: Cobalt-blue glass filter.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Most vigorous with water: Li, Na or K?

  1. Reactivity rises down Group 1.
  2. K (ignites instantly).

Answer: K.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reporting Ca as apple-green (that is Ba).
  • Expecting Be to behave like Ca.

Chapter 4 · Topic 22

Lithium anomalous behaviour

s-Block Elementss & p BasicsTopic 22 of 28

Explanation

Concept. In s-Block Elements, Lithium anomalous behaviour: Li copies Mg diagonally in nitrides and sparing solubilities. First-period elements (small, no d-orbitals, high EN) behave oddly; diagonal pairs Li-Mg and Be-Al resemble from similar charge/radius. Penetration s>p>d>f leaves d/f shielding poor, so Slater Zeff rises and lanthanides contract.
Key formula(s).\[ Li\!-\!Mg\,habits \]
Key points.
  • Inert pair: heavy p-block keeps ns2 unshared (Pb2+, Bi3+ stable).
  • Lanthanide contraction makes Zr/Hf and Nb/Ta near-twins.
  • Li-Mg and Be-Al diagonals share carbonates, nitrides, solubility habits.
  • Slater: same-shell electrons shield 0.35 (1s: 0.30); inner shells ~0.85-1.0.
Example 1.

Using Slater rules, estimate Zeff for a 3s electron of Mg (Z=12, config 1s2 2s2p8 3s2).

  1. S = 8(1.0) + 2(0.35)... inner 1s,2s2p: 2(1.0)+8(0.85)+1(0.35) = 9.15.
  2. Zeff = 12-9.15 = 2.85.

Answer: About 2.85.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why are Zr and Hf chemically twins?

  1. Lanthanide contraction cancels the expected size jump.
  2. Nearly identical radii and chemistry.

Answer: Lanthanide contraction.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying Slater 0.35 to 1s electrons (use 0.30).
  • Blaming inert pair for light elements.

Explanation

Concept. In s-Block Elements, Sodium compounds: NaCl, Na2CO3 and NaOH anchor chlor-alkali industry. Li-Mg diagonal kinship (nitrides, less-soluble salts, stable... no - Li forms nitride like Mg); NaCl/KCl fertilisers, Na2CO3 washing soda, CaO/CaCO3 in cement; Na+/K+ pumps and Mg2+ chlorophyll plus Ca2+ bones run biology.
Key formula(s).\[ Na_2CO_3\,(Solvay),\;Li_3N\,only\,alkali\,nitride \]
Key points.
  • Washing soda Na2CO3.10H2O from Solvay (NH3 + CO2 + NaCl).
  • Plaster: CaSO4.1/2H2O sets with water to gypsum.
  • Na+/K+ ATPase keeps gradients; Ca2+ triggers muscles.
  • LiCl deliquescent like MgCl2; both give nitrides on heating in N2.
Example 1.

Only alkali metal forming a nitride: which and why?

  1. Tiny Li+ gives huge lattice energy with small N3-.
  2. Li (6Li + N2 -> 2Li3N), diagonal with Mg.

Answer: Li.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Washing soda formula and one use?

  1. Na2CO3.10H2O from Solvay process.
  2. Softening water / glass making.

Answer: Na2CO3.10H2O.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming all alkali metals form nitrides.
  • Confusing plaster (hemihydrate) with gypsum (dihydrate).

Chapter 5 · Topic 1

p-block electronic configuration

p-Block Elements - General Conceptss & p BasicsTopic 1 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In p-Block General Concepts, p-block electronic configuration: ns2np1-6 valence scripts across Groups 13-18. p-block spans metals to noble gases: catenation peaks at carbon, multiple bonds need small 2p overlap, oxides march basic-amphoteric-acidic, and heavy members cling to lower states (inert pair).
Key formula(s).\[ catenation:\,C>S>Si>P;\;oxide\,nature:\,basic\to amphoteric\to acidic,\;acid\,order:\,HClO_4 top \]
Key points.
  • Carbon catenates endlessly (strong C-C, good pi overlap); Si/P/S weakly.
  • Acid strength of oxyacids rises with central oxidation state.
  • Down groups oxidising power of +5/+4 falls while reducing power of +3 rises.
  • First-row anomaly: no d-orbitals caps covalence at 4.
Example 1.

Strongest catenation after carbon?

  1. Bond energies: S-S outlasts Si-Si and P-P.
  2. Sulphur.

Answer: Sulphur.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Acidic order: HClO4, H2SO4, H3PO4, H4SiO4?

  1. Higher central oxidation state = stronger acid.
  2. HClO4 > H2SO4 > H3PO4 > H4SiO4.

Answer: Descending with oxidation state.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Expecting Si to catenate like C.
  • Reversing oxyacid strength order.
Back to Index
Index / s & p Basics
Chapter 5 · Topic 2

General trends

p-Block Elements - General Conceptss & p BasicsTopic 2 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In p-Block General Concepts, General trends: metals fade to metalloids to non-metals across the block. p-block spans metals to noble gases: catenation peaks at carbon, multiple bonds need small 2p overlap, oxides march basic-amphoteric-acidic, and heavy members cling to lower states (inert pair).
Key formula(s).\[ catenation:\,C>S>Si>P;\;oxide\,nature:\,basic\to amphoteric\to acidic \]
Key points.
  • Acid strength of oxyacids rises with central oxidation state.
  • Down groups oxidising power of +5/+4 falls while reducing power of +3 rises.
  • First-row anomaly: no d-orbitals caps covalence at 4.
  • Carbon catenates endlessly (strong C-C, good pi overlap); Si/P/S weakly.
Example 1.

S-S vs O-O bond: which supports chains?

  1. S-S 266 kJ beats weak O-O peroxides.
  2. Sulphur catenates.

Answer: Sulphur.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Strongest acid: HClO4 or HIO4?

  1. Smaller Cl holds +7 tighter.
  2. HClO4.

Answer: HClO4.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Expecting Si to catenate like C.
  • Reversing oxyacid strength order.

Chapter 5 · Topic 4

Ionisation enthalpy

p-Block Elements - General Conceptss & p BasicsTopic 4 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In p-Block General Concepts, Ionisation enthalpy: ionisation energy tracks Zeff over size with core-break jumps. Ionisation enthalpy is the energy to remove one mole of gaseous electrons; it rises across periods and falls down groups, jumping after noble-gas cores and at half/full subshells.
Key formula(s).\[ IE_1 < IE_2 < IE_3,\;jumps\,at\,core\,breaks \]
Key points.
  • Successive IEs jump when the next electron comes from an inner shell (Mg: IE3 huge).
  • Anomalies: Be>B (s vs p removal), N>O (half-filled stability).
  • Down a group size wins over charge: IE falls.
  • Second IE of alkali metals is enormous (noble-gas core).
Example 1.

IE1, IE2, IE3 of X are 520, 7300, 11800 kJ/mol. Identify the group.

  1. Giant jump between IE1 and IE2 means one valence electron.
  2. Alkali metal (Group 1).

Answer: Group 1.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why is IE1(O) < IE1(N)?

  1. N has exactly half-filled 2p (extra stable).
  2. O loses a paired electron more easily.

Answer: Half-filled stability of N.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading kJ values without spotting the core-break jump.
  • Assuming IE always rises uniformly.
Back to Index
Index / s & p Basics
Chapter 5 · Topic 5

Electron gain enthalpy

p-Block Elements - General Conceptss & p BasicsTopic 5 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In p-Block General Concepts, Electron gain enthalpy: gain enthalpy peaks at Cl with N near zero. Electron gain enthalpy is the energy released adding an electron to a gaseous atom; most negative for Cl (not F, due to small-size repulsion), with N, Be, Mg near zero or positive.
Key formula(s).\[ \Delta_{eg}H:\,Cl > F > Br > I \]
Key points.
  • Half-filled (N) and full (Be, noble) shells resist addition.
  • O < S for the same size reason as F < Cl.
  • Second electron gain is always endothermic (repulsion).
  • F loses to Cl because the compact 2p repels the incoming electron.
Example 1.

Why is electron gain of Cl more exothermic than F?

  1. F 2p is tiny; electron-electron repulsion offsets nuclear pull.
  2. Cl 3p is roomier, so net release is larger.

Answer: Small-orbital repulsion in F.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which has positive electron gain enthalpy: N or P?

  1. N 2p is half-filled and compact.
  2. N resists (positive); P is slightly exothermic.

Answer: N.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Blindly ranking F first in electron gain.
  • Confusing sign (exothermic = negative).
Back to Index
Index / s & p Basics
Chapter 5 · Topic 6

Electronegativity

p-Block Elements - General Conceptss & p BasicsTopic 6 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In p-Block General Concepts, Electronegativity: electronegativity pull peaks at fluorine and orders bond character. Electronegativity is an atom's pull on bond electrons: F (4.0) > O > Cl > N on Pauling scale, rising across periods and falling down groups; Mulliken averages IE and EA while Allred-Rochow uses Zeff over r-squared.
Key formula(s).\[ \chi_M=\frac{IE+EA}{2},\;\chi_{AR}\propto\frac{Z_{eff}}{r^2} \]
Key points.
  • Across a period EN rises with Zeff; down a group size dilutes pull.
  • Diagonal pairs (Li-Mg, Be-Al) match in EN.
  • EN difference predicts bond character: >1.7 largely ionic.
  • Noble gases are skipped (no bonds to compare).
Example 1.

Most ionic among NaCl, MgCl2, AlCl3 by EN reasoning?

  1. Cation EN rises Na < Mg < Al, so difference shrinks.
  2. NaCl is most ionic.

Answer: NaCl.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why do BeCl2 and AlCl3 show covalent character?

  1. Small highly-charged cations polarise Cl- (Fajan).
  2. EN gap effectively narrows.

Answer: Polarisation by small cations.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning EN to noble gases.
  • Using EN difference as the only ionic test.
Back to Index
Index / s & p Basics
Chapter 5 · Topic 7

Oxidation states

p-Block Elements - General Conceptss & p BasicsTopic 7 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In p-Block General Concepts, Oxidation states: the working oxidation state follows valence count, locked low by the inert pair when heavy. Metallic character (electropositive, basic oxides, reducing) rises down and left; non-metallic rises up and right. Periodicity repeats because valence shells repeat; blocks s/p/d/f follow the filling subshell.
Key formula(s).\[ group\,oxidation\,state = valence\,count \]
Key points.
  • Oxides: basic (metals) to amphoteric to acidic (non-metals) across a period.
  • Valency for s/p = group number or 8 minus it.
  • Period number = principal quantum number of valence shell.
  • Long form fixes Mendeleev anomalies (Ar-K, Co-Ni, Te-I) by atomic number.
Example 1.

Most metallic among Si, Al, P, S?

  1. Metallic character falls left to right.
  2. Al (Group 13, leftmost).

Answer: Al.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Nature of Al2O3 vs Na2O vs Cl2O7?

  1. Na2O basic, Al2O3 amphoteric, Cl2O7 strongly acidic.
  2. Basic to acidic across the period.

Answer: Basic, amphoteric, acidic.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling Al2O3 purely basic.
  • Mixing period number with group number.
Back to Index
Index / s & p Basics
Chapter 5 · Topic 8

Inert pair effect

p-Block Elements - General Conceptss & p BasicsTopic 8 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In p-Block General Concepts, Inert pair effect: heavy p-blockers hoard ns2, stabilising lower oxidation states. First-period elements (small, no d-orbitals, high EN) behave oddly; diagonal pairs Li-Mg and Be-Al resemble from similar charge/radius. Penetration s>p>d>f leaves d/f shielding poor, so Slater Zeff rises and lanthanides contract.
Key formula(s).\[ Li\!-\!Mg\,habits,\;0.35/0.85\,Slater \]
Key points.
  • Slater: same-shell electrons shield 0.35 (1s: 0.30); inner shells ~0.85-1.0.
  • Inert pair: heavy p-block keeps ns2 unshared (Pb2+, Bi3+ stable).
  • Lanthanide contraction makes Zr/Hf and Nb/Ta near-twins.
  • Li-Mg and Be-Al diagonals share carbonates, nitrides, solubility habits.
Example 1.

Using Slater rules, estimate Zeff for a 3s electron of Mg (Z=12, config 1s2 2s2p8 3s2).

  1. S = 8(1.0) + 2(0.35)... inner 1s,2s2p: 2(1.0)+8(0.85)+1(0.35) = 9.15.
  2. Zeff = 12-9.15 = 2.85.

Answer: About 2.85.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why are Zr and Hf chemically twins?

  1. Lanthanide contraction cancels the expected size jump.
  2. Nearly identical radii and chemistry.

Answer: Lanthanide contraction.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying Slater 0.35 to 1s electrons (use 0.30).
  • Blaming inert pair for light elements.

Chapter 5 · Topic 14

Redox behaviour

p-Block Elements - General Conceptss & p BasicsTopic 14 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In p-Block General Concepts, Redox behaviour: upper states oxidise, lower states reduce across p-block. p-block spans metals to noble gases: catenation peaks at carbon, multiple bonds need small 2p overlap, oxides march basic-amphoteric-acidic, and heavy members cling to lower states (inert pair).
Key formula(s).\[ upper\,oxidises,\,lower\,reduces \]
Key points.
  • Acid strength of oxyacids rises with central oxidation state.
  • Down groups oxidising power of +5/+4 falls while reducing power of +3 rises.
  • First-row anomaly: no d-orbitals caps covalence at 4.
  • Carbon catenates endlessly (strong C-C, good pi overlap); Si/P/S weakly.
Example 1.

S-S vs O-O bond: which supports chains?

  1. S-S 266 kJ beats weak O-O peroxides.
  2. Sulphur catenates.

Answer: Sulphur.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Strongest acid: HClO4 or HIO4?

  1. Smaller Cl holds +7 tighter.
  2. HClO4.

Answer: HClO4.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Expecting Si to catenate like C.
  • Reversing oxyacid strength order.

Chapter 5 · Topic 19

Stability of oxidation states

p-Block Elements - General Conceptss & p BasicsTopic 19 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In p-Block General Concepts, Stability of oxidation states: light members hold group states, heavy ones sink to inert-pair states. Metallic character (electropositive, basic oxides, reducing) rises down and left; non-metallic rises up and right. Periodicity repeats because valence shells repeat; blocks s/p/d/f follow the filling subshell.
Key formula(s).\[ metallic:\,Fr > Cs > \dots > F\,(least),\;group\,oxidation\,state = valence\,count \]
Key points.
  • Oxides: basic (metals) to amphoteric to acidic (non-metals) across a period.
  • Valency for s/p = group number or 8 minus it.
  • Period number = principal quantum number of valence shell.
  • Long form fixes Mendeleev anomalies (Ar-K, Co-Ni, Te-I) by atomic number.
Example 1.

Most metallic among Si, Al, P, S?

  1. Metallic character falls left to right.
  2. Al (Group 13, leftmost).

Answer: Al.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Nature of Al2O3 vs Na2O vs Cl2O7?

  1. Na2O basic, Al2O3 amphoteric, Cl2O7 strongly acidic.
  2. Basic to acidic across the period.

Answer: Basic, amphoteric, acidic.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling Al2O3 purely basic.
  • Mixing period number with group number.

Chapter 6 · Topic 1

Electronic configuration

Group 13 - Boron Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 1 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Group 13 - Boron Family, Electronic configuration: the valence-shell script fixes group, period and chemistry at once. Boron stays electron-deficient (banana bridges, back-bonded halides) while aluminium turns amphoteric and dimerises its chloride.
Key formula(s).\[ BBr_3>BCl_3>BF_3,\;Al_2Cl_6\,dimer \]
Key points.
  • Back-bonding weakens BF3 acidity.
  • Borax beads test metals.
  • Al2O3 + base gives aluminate.
  • 2 banana bonds per B2H6.
Example 1.

Terminal B-H count in B2H6?

  1. 4 terminal + 2 bridges.
  2. 4 terminal.

Answer: 4.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) AlCl3 in acidified water: product?

  1. Gives [Al(H2O)6]3+.
  2. Hexaaqua ion.

Answer: [Al(H2O)6]3+.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • BF3 strongest-acid myth.
  • Flat diborane drawing.

Chapter 6 · Topic 2

Atomic size and trends

Group 13 - Boron Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 2 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Group 13 - Boron Family, Atomic size and trends: size and IE trends wobble at d-block and inert-pair steps. Boron chemistry runs electron-deficient: B2H6 with 3c-2e banana bridges, BF3/BCl3 Lewis acids (BCl3 > BF3 by back-bonding), borax-boric-acid buffers, and AlCl3 dimers with amphoteric Al2O3.
Key formula(s).\[ acidity:\,BBr_3>BCl_3>BF_3,\;AlCl_3\,dimer\,Al_2Cl_6 \]
Key points.
  • Borax Na2B4O7.10H2O gives metaborate beads in bead test.
  • Al2O3 amphoteric: dissolves in NaOH (aluminate) and acids.
  • Banana bonds: 2 bridging H in 3-centre-2-electron links.
  • BF3 weakest Lewis acid (p-pi back donation fills B); BBr3 strongest.
Example 1.

How many 3c-2e bonds in diborane?

  1. Two B-H-B bridges.
  2. 2 banana bonds (+ 4 normal terminal B-H).

Answer: Two.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Strongest Lewis acid: BF3 or BCl3?

  1. Back-bonding order B-F > B-Cl fills boron most in BF3.
  2. BCl3 stronger acid.

Answer: BCl3.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling BF3 the strongest boron acid.
  • Drawing diborane with only normal bonds.

Chapter 6 · Topic 4

Inert pair effect

Group 13 - Boron Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 4 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Group 13 - Boron Family, Inert pair effect: heavy p-blockers hoard ns2, stabilising lower oxidation states. First-period elements (small, no d-orbitals, high EN) behave oddly; diagonal pairs Li-Mg and Be-Al resemble from similar charge/radius. Penetration s>p>d>f leaves d/f shielding poor, so Slater Zeff rises and lanthanides contract.
Key formula(s).\[ Z_{eff}=Z-S,\;penetration:\,s>p>d>f \]
Key points.
  • Slater: same-shell electrons shield 0.35 (1s: 0.30); inner shells ~0.85-1.0.
  • Inert pair: heavy p-block keeps ns2 unshared (Pb2+, Bi3+ stable).
  • Lanthanide contraction makes Zr/Hf and Nb/Ta near-twins.
  • Li-Mg and Be-Al diagonals share carbonates, nitrides, solubility habits.
Example 1.

Using Slater rules, estimate Zeff for a 3s electron of Mg (Z=12, config 1s2 2s2p8 3s2).

  1. S = 8(1.0) + 2(0.35)... inner 1s,2s2p: 2(1.0)+8(0.85)+1(0.35) = 9.15.
  2. Zeff = 12-9.15 = 2.85.

Answer: About 2.85.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why are Zr and Hf chemically twins?

  1. Lanthanide contraction cancels the expected size jump.
  2. Nearly identical radii and chemistry.

Answer: Lanthanide contraction.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying Slater 0.35 to 1s electrons (use 0.30).
  • Blaming inert pair for light elements.

Chapter 6 · Topic 13

Aluminium

Group 13 - Boron Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 13 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Group 13 - Boron Family, Aluminium: amphoteric aluminium bridges metal and non-metal chemistry. Boron chemistry runs electron-deficient: B2H6 with 3c-2e banana bridges, BF3/BCl3 Lewis acids (BCl3 > BF3 by back-bonding), borax-boric-acid buffers, and AlCl3 dimers with amphoteric Al2O3.
Key formula(s).\[ Al_2O_3\,amphoteric \]
Key points.
  • BF3 weakest Lewis acid (p-pi back donation fills B); BBr3 strongest.
  • Borax Na2B4O7.10H2O gives metaborate beads in bead test.
  • Al2O3 amphoteric: dissolves in NaOH (aluminate) and acids.
  • Banana bonds: 2 bridging H in 3-centre-2-electron links.
Example 1.

Why does AlCl3 fume in moist air?

  1. Hydrolyses to HCl fumes.
  2. AlCl3 + 3H2O -> Al(OH)3 + 3HCl.

Answer: HCl fumes.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Borax bead green in flame: metal?

  1. Copper metaborate tints green-blue.
  2. Copper (chromium also green-cold).

Answer: Cu/Cr.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.

  • Drawing diborane with only normal bonds.

Chapter 7 · Topic 1

Electronic configuration

Group 14 - Carbon Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 1 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Group 14 - Carbon Family, Electronic configuration: the valence-shell script fixes group, period and chemistry at once. Silicon builds SiO4 networks (silicates, zeolite cages, silicone -Si-O- polymers, carborundum SiC abrasive) while lead abandons +4 for stable +2 (PbO2 oxidant, Pb3O4 red lead, PbCl4 fuming covalent).
Key formula(s).\[ silicone:\,R_2SiO\,repeat,\;zeolite\,sieves \]
Key points.
  • PbCl4 covalent fumes; PbCl2 ionic stable - Pb4+ oxidises Cl-.
  • SiC is nearly diamond-hard (abrasive).
  • Zeolites (ZSM-5) sieve molecules and soften water by ion exchange.
  • Silicones: water-repellent, heat-stable (R2SiCl2 hydrolysis product).
Example 1.

Why is PbCl4 unstable while CCl4 is stable?

  1. Inert pair: Pb4+ craves reduction to Pb2+.
  2. PbCl4 collapses to PbCl2 + Cl2.

Answer: Inert-pair driven reduction.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Basic unit of silicates?

  1. SiO4 tetrahedron sharing corners.
  2. SiO4 4- unit.

Answer: SiO4 tetrahedron.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Expecting Si to double-bond like C freely.
  • Treating Pb4+ as stable as Sn4+.

Chapter 7 · Topic 3

Oxidation states

Group 14 - Carbon Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 3 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Group 14 - Carbon Family, Oxidation states: the working oxidation state follows valence count, locked low by the inert pair when heavy. Metallic character (electropositive, basic oxides, reducing) rises down and left; non-metallic rises up and right. Periodicity repeats because valence shells repeat; blocks s/p/d/f follow the filling subshell.
Key formula(s).\[ group\,oxidation\,state = valence\,count \]
Key points.
  • Valency for s/p = group number or 8 minus it.
  • Period number = principal quantum number of valence shell.
  • Long form fixes Mendeleev anomalies (Ar-K, Co-Ni, Te-I) by atomic number.
  • Oxides: basic (metals) to amphoteric to acidic (non-metals) across a period.
Example 1.

Most non-metallic: Si, P, S, Cl?

  1. Rises right across the period.
  2. Cl.

Answer: Cl.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Amphoteric oxides among Na2O, Al2O3, SO2?

  1. Middle-period oxide reacts both ways.
  2. Al2O3.

Answer: Al2O3.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling Al2O3 purely basic.
  • Mixing period number with group number.

Chapter 7 · Topic 5

Catenation

Group 14 - Carbon Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 5 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Group 14 - Carbon Family, Catenation: self-linking peaks at carbon and fades down groups. p-block spans metals to noble gases: catenation peaks at carbon, multiple bonds need small 2p overlap, oxides march basic-amphoteric-acidic, and heavy members cling to lower states (inert pair).
Key formula(s).\[ catenation:\,C>S>Si>P;\;oxide\,nature:\,basic\to amphoteric\to acidic \]
Key points.
  • Carbon catenates endlessly (strong C-C, good pi overlap); Si/P/S weakly.
  • Acid strength of oxyacids rises with central oxidation state.
  • Down groups oxidising power of +5/+4 falls while reducing power of +3 rises.
  • First-row anomaly: no d-orbitals caps covalence at 4.
Example 1.

Strongest catenation after carbon?

  1. Bond energies: S-S outlasts Si-Si and P-P.
  2. Sulphur.

Answer: Sulphur.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Acidic order: HClO4, H2SO4, H3PO4, H4SiO4?

  1. Higher central oxidation state = stronger acid.
  2. HClO4 > H2SO4 > H3PO4 > H4SiO4.

Answer: Descending with oxidation state.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Expecting Si to catenate like C.
  • Reversing oxyacid strength order.
Back to Index
Index / p-Block Families
Chapter 7 · Topic 6

Allotropes of carbon

Group 14 - Carbon Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 6 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Group 14 - Carbon Family, Allotropes of carbon: diamond, graphite, fullerene and graphene rewire the same element. Carbon allotropes rewire sp3 diamond (hard insulator), sp2 graphite/graphene (layer conductor, lubricant) and C60 balls; CO triple-bonds with a lone pair on C (strong reductant, toxic ligand) while CO2 linear double bonds dissolve to carbonic acid.
Key formula(s).\[ diamond\,sp^3,\;graphite\,sp^2\,layers \]
Key points.
  • CO poisoning: binds haemoglobin ~250x stronger than O2.
  • CO2 is linear non-polar; dry ice sublimes.
  • Fullerene C60 has 12 pentagons + 20 hexagons.
  • Graphite conducts along layers (delocalised pi), diamond not at all.
Example 1.

Donor atom in metal carbonyls: C or O?

  1. HOMO sits on carbon lone pair.
  2. Carbon end binds.

Answer: Carbon.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Dry ice sublimes at?

  1. CO2(s) to gas directly.
  2. -78 C.

Answer: -78 C.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning sp3 to graphite carbons.
  • Calling CO2 polar.

Chapter 7 · Topic 7

Diamond

Group 14 - Carbon Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 7 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Group 14 - Carbon Family, Diamond: sp3 diamond is the hardest insulating network. Carbon allotropes rewire sp3 diamond (hard insulator), sp2 graphite/graphene (layer conductor, lubricant) and C60 balls; CO triple-bonds with a lone pair on C (strong reductant, toxic ligand) while CO2 linear double bonds dissolve to carbonic acid.
Key formula(s).\[ diamond\,sp^3,\;CO_2+ H_2O\\rightleftharpoons H_2CO_3 \]
Key points.
  • CO2 is linear non-polar; dry ice sublimes.
  • Fullerene C60 has 12 pentagons + 20 hexagons.
  • Graphite conducts along layers (delocalised pi), diamond not at all.
  • CO poisoning: binds haemoglobin ~250x stronger than O2.
Example 1.

Why does graphite conduct but diamond not?

  1. Graphite sp2 leaves one p electron delocalised per C along sheets.
  2. Diamond locks all four in sigma bonds.

Answer: Delocalised pi system in graphite.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) CO is a strong reductant in blast furnace. Write its key role.

  1. Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2 in the stack.
  2. CO strips oxygen as CO2.

Answer: Reduces iron oxides to Fe.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning sp3 to graphite carbons.
  • Calling CO2 polar.

Chapter 7 · Topic 13

Reducing property of CO

Group 14 - Carbon Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 13 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Group 14 - Carbon Family, Reducing property of CO: CO strips oxide oxygen as CO2 in furnaces. Carbon allotropes rewire sp3 diamond (hard insulator), sp2 graphite/graphene (layer conductor, lubricant) and C60 balls; CO triple-bonds with a lone pair on C (strong reductant, toxic ligand) while CO2 linear double bonds dissolve to carbonic acid.
Key formula(s).\[ diamond\,sp^3,\;CO:\,:C\\equiv O:^+,\;CO_2+ H_2O\\rightleftharpoons H_2CO_3,\;graphene\,ballistic \]
Key points.
  • CO2 is linear non-polar; dry ice sublimes.
  • Fullerene C60 has 12 pentagons + 20 hexagons.
  • Graphite conducts along layers (delocalised pi), diamond not at all.
  • CO poisoning: binds haemoglobin ~250x stronger than O2.
Example 1.

Why does graphite conduct but diamond not?

  1. Graphite sp2 leaves one p electron delocalised per C along sheets.
  2. Diamond locks all four in sigma bonds.

Answer: Delocalised pi system in graphite.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) CO is a strong reductant in blast furnace. Write its key role.

  1. Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2 in the stack.
  2. CO strips oxygen as CO2.

Answer: Reduces iron oxides to Fe.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning sp3 to graphite carbons.
  • Calling CO2 polar.

Chapter 7 · Topic 16

Silicon

Group 14 - Carbon Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 16 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Group 14 - Carbon Family, Silicon: tetravalent silicon networks into semiconductors and silicates. Silicon builds SiO4 networks (silicates, zeolite cages, silicone -Si-O- polymers, carborundum SiC abrasive) while lead abandons +4 for stable +2 (PbO2 oxidant, Pb3O4 red lead, PbCl4 fuming covalent).
Key formula(s).\[ PbCl_4\,fumes\,+\,falls \],\;SiO_4\,tetrahedra\,share\,corners \]
Key points.
  • PbCl4 covalent fumes; PbCl2 ionic stable - Pb4+ oxidises Cl-.
  • SiC is nearly diamond-hard (abrasive).
  • Zeolites (ZSM-5) sieve molecules and soften water by ion exchange.
  • Silicones: water-repellent, heat-stable (R2SiCl2 hydrolysis product).
Example 1.

Why is PbCl4 unstable while CCl4 is stable?

  1. Inert pair: Pb4+ craves reduction to Pb2+.
  2. PbCl4 collapses to PbCl2 + Cl2.

Answer: Inert-pair driven reduction.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Basic unit of silicates?

  1. SiO4 tetrahedron sharing corners.
  2. SiO4 4- unit.

Answer: SiO4 tetrahedron.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Expecting Si to double-bond like C freely.
  • Treating Pb4+ as stable as Sn4+.

Chapter 8 · Topic 1

Electronic configuration

Group 15 - Nitrogen Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 1 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Group 15 - Nitrogen Family, Electronic configuration: the valence-shell script fixes group, period and chemistry at once. Group 15 runs Haber/Ostwald industry, N-oxide ladders and P oxoacids whose basicity counts P-OH only.
Key formula(s).\[ basicity=H_3PO_2(1),H_3PO_3(2),H_3PO_4(3),\;NO_2\\rightleftharpoons N_2O_4 \]
Key points.
  • White P under water.
  • PCl5(s) is ionic.
  • Aqua regia 3:1 HCl:HNO3.
  • NH3 out-basifies PH3.
Example 1.

P-OH groups in H3PO3?

  1. One P-H, two P-OH.
  2. 2 (dibasic).

Answer: 2.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) N2O + H2O product?

  1. N2O neutral, no reaction.
  2. No reaction.

Answer: Neutral oxide.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • All-H acidic counting.
  • White P in air.

Chapter 8 · Topic 2

Periodic trends

Group 15 - Nitrogen Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 2 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Group 15 - Nitrogen Family, Periodic trends: size, IE, EA and EN march together on Zeff versus shell number. Metallic character (electropositive, basic oxides, reducing) rises down and left; non-metallic rises up and right. Periodicity repeats because valence shells repeat; blocks s/p/d/f follow the filling subshell.
Key formula(s).\[ group\,oxidation\,state = valence\,count,\;period=shell \]
Key points.
  • Valency for s/p = group number or 8 minus it.
  • Period number = principal quantum number of valence shell.
  • Long form fixes Mendeleev anomalies (Ar-K, Co-Ni, Te-I) by atomic number.
  • Oxides: basic (metals) to amphoteric to acidic (non-metals) across a period.
Example 1.

Most non-metallic: Si, P, S, Cl?

  1. Rises right across the period.
  2. Cl.

Answer: Cl.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Amphoteric oxides among Na2O, Al2O3, SO2?

  1. Middle-period oxide reacts both ways.
  2. Al2O3.

Answer: Al2O3.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling Al2O3 purely basic.
  • Mixing period number with group number.

Most metallic among Si, Al, P, S?

Chapter 8 · Topic 4

Nitrogen anomalous behaviour

Group 15 - Nitrogen Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 4 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Group 15 - Nitrogen Family, Nitrogen anomalous behaviour: triple-bonded N2 is inert where P4 ignites. NH3 (Haber: N2 + 3H2 over Fe at 450 C/200 atm) is pyramidal basic (lone pair) forming ammine complexes; HNO3 (Ostwald: NH3 -> NO -> NO2 -> acid) passivates Al/Cr/Fe and oxidises with concentration-dependent products.
Key formula(s).\[ Haber:\,N_2+3H_2\\rightleftharpoons2NH_3,\;Ostwald:\,4NH_3+5O_2\to4NO \]
Key points.
  • NH3 basic order: NH3 > PH3 > AsH3 (lone-pair availability).
  • Conc HNO3 + Cu gives NO2; dilute gives NO/N2O by metal.
  • Aqua regia (3:1 HCl:HNO3) dissolves Au/Pt via nascent Cl2 + complexation.
  • N2 inertness is the triple-bond price (941 kJ/mol).
Example 1.

Why is NH3 more basic than PH3?

  1. Lone pair sits in compact sp3 on small N.
  2. Denser electron availability than diffuse P.

Answer: Compact N lone pair.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Cu + conc HNO3 vs dilute HNO3 products?

  1. Conc: Cu + 4HNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO2 + 2H2O.
  2. Dilute: 3Cu + 8HNO3 -> nitrates + 2NO.

Answer: NO2 vs NO.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using 1:3 instead of 3:1 for aqua regia.
  • Forgetting passivation of Al/Fe in conc HNO3.
