Chapter 8 · Topic 16

Nitrogen oxides

Group 15 - Nitrogen Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 16 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Group 15 - Nitrogen Family, Nitrogen oxides: N2O through N2O5 march oxidation states +1 to +5. Nitrogen oxides march N2O (+1, laughing gas) to N2O5 (+5, anhydride of HNO3) with NO2/N2O4 dimer equilibrium; phosphorus glows white (P4, pyrophoric) to polymeric red/black, gives PH3, hydrolysing PCl5, and oxoacids whose basicity equals P-H-free OH count.
Key formula(s).\[ basicity:\,H_3PO_2=1,\,H_3PO_3=2,\,H_3PO_4=3,\;N_2O_5\,(+5)\,nitric\,anhydride \]
Key points.
  • White P stored under water (ignites in air); red is polymeric and safer.
  • PCl5(s) is ionic [PCl4]+[PCl6]-; PCl5 hydrolyses fully to H3PO4.
  • H3PO2 (1 P-OH... 1 replaceable H) is monobasic; H3PO3 dibasic.
  • N2O5 + H2O -> 2HNO3 (anhydride link).
Example 1.

Basicities of H3PO2, H3PO3, H3PO4?

  1. Count P-OH groups: 1, 2, 3 (P-H bonds do not ionise).
  2. 1, 2, 3.

Answer: Mono, di, tribasic.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Brown gas that dimerises colourless on cooling?

  1. 2NO2 (brown) <=> N2O4 (colourless), exothermic forward... dimer favoured cold.
  2. NO2/N2O4 pair.

Answer: NO2 dimerises to N2O4.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Counting all H as acidic in P oxoacids.
  • Storing white phosphorus in air.

Chapter 9 · Topic 1

Electronic configuration

Group 16 - Oxygen Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 1 of 27

Explanation

Concept. In Group 16 - Oxygen Family, Electronic configuration: the valence-shell script fixes group, period and chemistry at once. Group 16 centres O3 resonance, H2S analysis, S8 rings and contact-process sulphuric acid via oleum.
Key formula(s).\[ O:[He]2s^22p^4,\;S:[Ne]3s^23p^4 \]
Key points.
  • H2S acid-gated for Group II.
  • Hot conc H2SO4 oxidises Cu.

  • O3 bent 117 deg.
Example 1.

Oleum 104.5%: free SO3?

  1. 4.5% water-equivalent... free SO3 about 20%.
  2. ~20% free SO3.

Answer: ~20%.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Rhombic-monoclinic transition T?

  1. S8 flips at 96 C.
  2. 96 C.

Answer: 96 C.

Chapter 9 · Topic 2

Periodic trends

Group 16 - Oxygen Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 2 of 27

Explanation

Concept. In Group 16 - Oxygen Family, Periodic trends: size, IE, EA and EN march together on Zeff versus shell number. Metallic character (electropositive, basic oxides, reducing) rises down and left; non-metallic rises up and right. Periodicity repeats because valence shells repeat; blocks s/p/d/f follow the filling subshell.
Key formula(s).\[ group\,oxidation\,state = valence\,count,\;period=shell \]
Key points.
  • Period number = principal quantum number of valence shell.
  • Long form fixes Mendeleev anomalies (Ar-K, Co-Ni, Te-I) by atomic number.
  • Oxides: basic (metals) to amphoteric to acidic (non-metals) across a period.
  • Valency for s/p = group number or 8 minus it.
Example 1.

Most metallic among Si, Al, P, S?

  1. Metallic character falls left to right.
  2. Al (Group 13, leftmost).

Answer: Al.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Nature of Al2O3 vs Na2O vs Cl2O7?

  1. Na2O basic, Al2O3 amphoteric, Cl2O7 strongly acidic.
  2. Basic to acidic across the period.

Answer: Basic, amphoteric, acidic.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling Al2O3 purely basic.
  • Mixing period number with group number.

Chapter 9 · Topic 4

Oxygen anomalous behaviour

Group 16 - Oxygen Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 4 of 27

Explanation

Concept. In Group 16 - Oxygen Family, Oxygen anomalous behaviour: tiny O double-bonds where S catenates. O2 (paramagnetic double bond) is made by heating KClO3/MnO2 or peroxides; O3 bent (117 deg, resonance 1.5 order) is made in ozonisers, oxidises everything (tail-gas Hg test), and shields UV as the ozone layer.
Key formula(s).\[ O_3\,screens\,UV \],\;O_3\,bent\,117^\\circ \]
Key points.
  • Mercury loses meniscus with O3 (tailing test).
  • Bond order in O3 is 1.5 per O-O link.
  • O2 paramagnetism proves MOT over Lewis.
  • O3 estimated by KI titration (I2 liberated).
Example 1.

O3 + KI (buffered) liberates?

  1. O3 oxidises I- to I2.
  2. Iodine (titrated).

Answer: I2.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) O-O bond order in O3?

  1. Resonance over 3 centres, 4 pi... 1.5 each.
  2. 1.5.

Answer: 1.5.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Drawing O3 linear.
  • Missing resonance in O-O length.

Example 1.

Shape and bond angle of ozone?

Answer: Bent, 117 deg.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Tailing of mercury test indicates?

  1. O3 oxidises Hg surface to Hg2O.
  2. Ozone present.

Answer: O3.

Chapter 9 · Topic 12

Hydrogen sulphide

Group 16 - Oxygen Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 12 of 27

Explanation

Concept. In Group 16 - Oxygen Family, Hydrogen sulphide: rotten-egg H2S is a weak acid and group reagent. H2S (Kipp: FeS + acid) is a weak diprotic acid and group-II precipitant; S8 rings flip rhombic to monoclinic at 96 C; SO2 bleaches by reduction; contact-process H2SO4 (V2O5, oleum H2S2O7 intermediate) chars organics and oxidises hot.
Key formula(s).\[ Kipp:\,FeS+acid,\;acid\,gates\,Group\,II\,only \]
Key points.
  • H2S in acidic medium precipitates Group II sulphides selectively.
  • Oleum strength: % = 100 + 20x/18... 109% H2SO4 means 9% free SO3 logic.
  • Hot conc H2SO4 oxidises Cu/C (SO2 released); cold conc only dehydrates.
  • Hypo Na2S2O3 fixes photography (AgBr complexation).
Example 1.

Why is H2S passed in acidic medium for Group II analysis?

  1. Acid suppresses S2- via common ion, keeping ion product low.
  2. Only very-low-Ksp sulphides (Group II) precipitate.

Answer: Selectivity via suppressed S2-.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Catalyst in the contact process?

  1. V2O5 at ~450 C oxidises SO2 to SO3.
  2. Vanadium pentoxide.

Answer: V2O5.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Confusing oleum percent with water content.
  • Calling cold conc H2SO4 an oxidant for Cu.

Chapter 9 · Topic 24

Oxoacids of sulphur

Group 16 - Oxygen Familyp-Block FamiliesTopic 24 of 27

Explanation

Concept. In Group 16 - Oxygen Family, Oxoacids of sulphur: sulphurous to peroxo acids span S oxidation states. H2S (Kipp: FeS + acid) is a weak diprotic acid and group-II precipitant; S8 rings flip rhombic to monoclinic at 96 C; SO2 bleaches by reduction; contact-process H2SO4 (V2O5, oleum H2S2O7 intermediate) chars organics and oxidises hot.
Key formula(s).\[ acid\,gates\,Group\,II\,only \]
Key points.
  • H2S in acidic medium precipitates Group II sulphides selectively.
  • Oleum strength: % = 100 + 20x/18... 109% H2SO4 means 9% free SO3 logic.
  • Hot conc H2SO4 oxidises Cu/C (SO2 released); cold conc only dehydrates.
  • Hypo Na2S2O3 fixes photography (AgBr complexation).
Example 1.

Why is H2S passed in acidic medium for Group II analysis?

  1. Acid suppresses S2- via common ion, keeping ion product low.
  2. Only very-low-Ksp sulphides (Group II) precipitate.

Answer: Selectivity via suppressed S2-.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Catalyst in the contact process?

  1. V2O5 at ~450 C oxidises SO2 to SO3.
  2. Vanadium pentoxide.

Answer: V2O5.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Confusing oleum percent with water content.
  • Calling cold conc H2SO4 an oxidant for Cu.

Chapter 10 · Topic 1

Electronic configuration

Group 17 - Halogensp-Block FamiliesTopic 1 of 24

Explanation

Concept. In Group 17 - Halogens, Electronic configuration: the valence-shell script fixes group, period and chemistry at once. Halogens oxidise down to I2, HX acidity avalanches down, and interhalogens take lone-pair-driven shapes.
Key formula(s).\[ ClF_3\,T \],\;F_2>Cl_2>Br_2>I_2\,(oxidising) \]
Key points.
  • Bleaching is permanent oxidation.
  • Pseudohalogens mimic X2.
  • HF etches glass.
  • Cl2/base splits by temperature.
Example 1.

Shape of BrF5?

  1. 5 bonds + 1 lone pair: octahedral set.
  2. Square pyramidal.

Answer: Square pyramidal.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Disproportionation in cold NaOH + Cl2?

  1. Cl- + ClO- cold.
  2. Chloride + hypochlorite.

Answer: Cl-/ClO-.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Axial lone pairs in TBP.
  • SO2 bleaching called permanent.

Chapter 10 · Topic 2

Periodic trends

Group 17 - Halogensp-Block FamiliesTopic 2 of 24

Explanation

Concept. In Group 17 - Halogens, Periodic trends: size, IE, EA and EN march together on Zeff versus shell number. Metallic character (electropositive, basic oxides, reducing) rises down and left; non-metallic rises up and right. Periodicity repeats because valence shells repeat; blocks s/p/d/f follow the filling subshell.
Key formula(s).\[ group\,oxidation\,state = valence\,count,\;period=shell \]
Key points.
  • Oxides: basic (metals) to amphoteric to acidic (non-metals) across a period.
  • Valency for s/p = group number or 8 minus it.
  • Period number = principal quantum number of valence shell.
  • Long form fixes Mendeleev anomalies (Ar-K, Co-Ni, Te-I) by atomic number.
Example 1.

Most metallic among Si, Al, P, S?

  1. Metallic character falls left to right.
  2. Al (Group 13, leftmost).

Answer: Al.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Nature of Al2O3 vs Na2O vs Cl2O7?

  1. Na2O basic, Al2O3 amphoteric, Cl2O7 strongly acidic.
  2. Basic to acidic across the period.

Answer: Basic, amphoteric, acidic.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling Al2O3 purely basic.
  • Mixing period number with group number.

Chapter 10 · Topic 4

Fluorine anomalous behaviour

Group 17 - Halogensp-Block FamiliesTopic 4 of 24

Explanation

Concept. In Group 17 - Halogens, Fluorine anomalous behaviour: smallest F is the fiercest oxidant with weak F-F bond. Halogens oxidise strongest at F2 down to weakest I2 (bond energy quirk: Cl2 > F2 from lone-pair repulsion); HX acidity avalanches HF << HCl < HBr < HI while HF alone etches glass and H-bonds.
Key formula(s).\[ I_2\,needs\,oxidant \]
Key points.
  • F2 most reactive from low BDE + high hydration of F-.
  • I2 needs oxidant to show oxidising action.
  • F2 oxidises water to O2/O3; Cl2 gives HCl + HOCl.
  • HF weak acid (H-bonded polymer) yet etches SiO2 to H2SiF6.
Example 1.

Strongest hydrohalic acid and why?

  1. Larger anion spreads charge; H-X bond weakens down the group.
  2. HI.

Answer: HI.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why is F2 a stronger oxidant despite lower bond energy logic?

  1. Low dissociation energy plus huge F- hydration overcompensate.
  2. Thermodynamics favour F2 reduction.

Answer: Hydration + BDE effects.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Ranking HF a strong acid.
  • Assuming BDE order F2 > Cl2.

Chapter 10 · Topic 10

Interhalogen compounds

Group 17 - Halogensp-Block FamiliesTopic 10 of 24

Explanation

Concept. In Group 17 - Halogens, Interhalogen compounds: XX-prime-n compounds hydrolyse to smaller-halogen oxyacids. Interhalogens XX'n (n odd: ClF3 T-shape, BrF5 square pyramidal, IF7 pentagonal bipyramidal) hydrolyse to the smaller halogen's oxyacid; Cl2 bleaches via nascent oxygen; HClO4 out-acids all with Cl2 disproportionating in base hot vs cold.
Key formula(s).\[ IF_7\,pent\!-\!bipyr,\;acid:\,HClO_4>HClO_3>HClO_2>HClO \]
Key points.
  • Pseudohalogens (CN)2, (SCN)2 mimic halogen redox.
  • Polyhalides: I3-, ICl2- stabilise big cations.
  • Cl2 + cold NaOH -> Cl- + ClO-; hot -> Cl- + ClO3- (disproportionation).
  • Bleaching is oxidation by nascent O (permanent).
Example 1.

Shape of ClF3?

  1. Cl has 3 bonds + 2 lone pairs: TBP with equatorial pairs.
  2. T-shaped.

Answer: T-shaped.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Cl2 with hot concentrated NaOH gives?

  1. Disproportionation favours chlorate hot.
  2. NaCl + NaClO3 + H2O.

Answer: Chloride + chlorate.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Putting lone pairs axial in ClF3.
  • Calling bleaching by SO2 permanent (it is temporary).

Chapter 11 · Topic 1

Electronic configuration

Group 18 - Noble Gasesp-Block FamiliesTopic 1 of 13

Explanation

Concept. In Group 18 - Noble Gases, Electronic configuration: the valence-shell script fixes group, period and chemistry at once. Xenon fluorinates and oxidises under excitation into VSEPR-predictable shapes that hydrolyse to XeO3.
Key formula(s).\[ XeF_2\,lin,\;XeF_4\,sq-pl \]
Key points.
  • Ni vessels resist F2.
  • XeO3 dry detonates.
  • He divers, Ne signs.
  • First compound XePtF6.
Example 1.

XeF6 + H2O excess product?

  1. Full hydrolysis to XeO3.
  2. XeO3 + HF.

Answer: XeO3.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Shape of XeOF2?

  1. 3 sigma + 2 lone pairs... T-shaped.
  2. T-shaped.

Answer: T-shaped.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • XeF2 bent claim.
  • Forgetting XeO3 hazard.

Chapter 11 · Topic 2

Periodic trends

Group 18 - Noble Gasesp-Block FamiliesTopic 2 of 13

Explanation

Concept. In Group 18 - Noble Gases, Periodic trends: size, IE, EA and EN march together on Zeff versus shell number. Metallic character (electropositive, basic oxides, reducing) rises down and left; non-metallic rises up and right. Periodicity repeats because valence shells repeat; blocks s/p/d/f follow the filling subshell.
Key formula(s).\[ group\,oxidation\,state = valence\,count,\;period=shell \]
Key points.
  • Valency for s/p = group number or 8 minus it.
  • Period number = principal quantum number of valence shell.
  • Long form fixes Mendeleev anomalies (Ar-K, Co-Ni, Te-I) by atomic number.
  • Oxides: basic (metals) to amphoteric to acidic (non-metals) across a period.
Example 1.

Most non-metallic: Si, P, S, Cl?

  1. Rises right across the period.
  2. Cl.

Answer: Cl.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Amphoteric oxides among Na2O, Al2O3, SO2?

  1. Middle-period oxide reacts both ways.
  2. Al2O3.

Answer: Al2O3.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling Al2O3 purely basic.
  • Mixing period number with group number.

Chapter 11 · Topic 3

Inertness of noble gases

Group 18 - Noble Gasesp-Block FamiliesTopic 3 of 13

Explanation

Concept. In Group 18 - Noble Gases, Inertness of noble gases: full shells and peak IE freeze noble reactivity. Noble gases idle on full shells and peak ionisation (He highest); only Xe/Kr react with F2/O2 under excitation: XeF2 linear, XeF4 square planar, XeF6 distorted octahedral, XeO3 pyramidal (explosive), XeOF4 square pyramidal.
Key formula(s).\[ full\,shells\,idle \]
Key points.
  • He/Ar shield welding; Ne signs; He-O2 for divers.
  • First compound: Bartlett XePtF6 (1962).
  • XeF2/4/6 from Xe + F2 ratios (1:1... heated, Ni vessels).
  • XeF6 hydrolyses stepwise to XeO3 (explosive dry).
Example 1.

Shape of XeF4?

  1. Xe: 4 bonds + 2 lone pairs, octahedral electron set.
  2. Square planar (pairs opposite).

Answer: Square planar.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) XeO3 hazard on heating?

  1. Dry XeO3 detonates.
  2. Highly explosive.

Answer: Explodes.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning XeF2 bent (it is linear).
  • Forgetting XeOF4 geometry (square pyramidal).

Key formula(s).\[ XeO_3\,pyr,\;hydrolysis\to Xe+O_2+HF \]
Key points.
  • He/Ar shield welding; Ne signs; He-O2 for divers.
  • First compound: Bartlett XePtF6 (1962).
  • XeF2/4/6 from Xe + F2 ratios (1:1... heated, Ni vessels).
  • XeF6 hydrolyses stepwise to XeO3 (explosive dry).
Example 1.

Shape of XeF4?

  1. Xe: 4 bonds + 2 lone pairs, octahedral electron set.
  2. Square planar (pairs opposite).

Answer: Square planar.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) XeO3 hazard on heating?

  1. Dry XeO3 detonates.
  2. Highly explosive.

Answer: Explodes.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning XeF2 bent (it is linear).
  • Forgetting XeOF4 geometry (square pyramidal).

Chapter 12 · Topic 1

Transition elements

d- and f-Block Elementsd-f & CoordinationTopic 1 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In d- and f-Block Elements, Transition elements: d-blockers vary states, colours and magnetism via d electrons. d-block metals show variable states, colour and magnetism from unpaired d electrons, complex formation, catalysis and interstitial alloys; size barely falls across a series from poor d shielding.
Key formula(s).\[ \mu_{spin}=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\,BM;\;colour\iff unpaired\,d\,e^-;\;states:\,max\,at\,middle \]
Key points.
  • Colour needs d-d transitions (unpaired); Zn2+/Sc3+ colourless.
  • Highest states with F/O (MnO4-, CrO3); low states with pi-acceptors.
  • Interstitials (Fe3C, TiH) harden steels.
  • Spin-only mu: n=1: 1.73, 2: 2.83, 3: 3.87, 4: 4.90, 5: 5.92 BM.
Example 1.

Highest oxidation state of Cr and Mn in fluorides/oxides?

  1. CrO3/CrF6 (+6); Mn2O7/MnO4- (+7).
  2. +6 and +7.

Answer: Cr +6, Mn +7.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why is Zn not a transition element strictly?

  1. Zn2+ is d10 in ground and stable states.
  2. No partially filled d.

Answer: d10 always.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Including orbital contribution in spin-only formula.
  • Expecting colour from d10 ions.

Chapter 12 · Topic 2

Electronic configuration

d- and f-Block Elementsd-f & CoordinationTopic 2 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In d- and f-Block Elements, Electronic configuration: the valence-shell script fixes group, period and chemistry at once. d-block runs variable states, spin-only magnetism, d-d colour and the MnO4-/Cr2O7 2- oxidant pair with medium-set n-factors.
Key formula(s).\[ MnO_4^-\,x=5/3/1 \],\;\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)} \]
Key points.
  • Acid KMnO4 1:5 with Fe2+.
  • Yellow-orange Cr pH flip.
  • Zn2+/Sc3+ colourless.
  • Middle members max states.
Example 1.

mu of Mn2+ high-spin?

  1. d5: n=5.
  2. 5.92 BM.

Answer: 5.92 BM.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) K2Cr2O7 : FeSO4 ratio in acid?

  1. Cr gains 6e total.
  2. 1:6.

Answer: 1:6.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Orbital moment in spin-only.
  • Mn x=5 in alkali.

Chapter 12 · Topic 6

Ionisation enthalpy

d- and f-Block Elementsd-f & CoordinationTopic 6 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In d- and f-Block Elements, Ionisation enthalpy: ionisation energy tracks Zeff over size with core-break jumps. Ionisation enthalpy is the energy to remove one mole of gaseous electrons; it rises across periods and falls down groups, jumping after noble-gas cores and at half/full subshells.
Key formula(s).\[ IE_1 < IE_2 < IE_3,\;jumps\,at\,core\,breaks \]
Key points.
  • Successive IEs jump when the next electron comes from an inner shell (Mg: IE3 huge).
  • Anomalies: Be>B (s vs p removal), N>O (half-filled stability).
  • Down a group size wins over charge: IE falls.
  • Second IE of alkali metals is enormous (noble-gas core).
Example 1.

IE1, IE2, IE3 of X are 520, 7300, 11800 kJ/mol. Identify the group.

  1. Giant jump between IE1 and IE2 means one valence electron.
  2. Alkali metal (Group 1).

Answer: Group 1.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why is IE1(O) < IE1(N)?

  1. N has exactly half-filled 2p (extra stable).
  2. O loses a paired electron more easily.

Answer: Half-filled stability of N.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading kJ values without spotting the core-break jump.
  • Assuming IE always rises uniformly.

  • Lanthanides separate by ion exchange (tiny size gaps).

  2. Cerium(IV).

Answer: Ce4+.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why is Th only +4 while U spans +3 to +6?

  1. Early actinides access 5f/6d/7s nearly degenerately.

Answer: Near-degenerate 5f-6d levels.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.

Explanation

Concept. Key formula(s).\[ \mu_{spin}=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\,BM;\;colour\iff unpaired\,d\,e^-;\;states:\,max\,at\,middle,\;Zn^{2+}\,d^{10},\,no\,colour,\;Cr^{+6},\,Mn^{+7}\,maxima,\;interstitials\,harden\,steel,\;alloys:\,matched\,sizes \]
Key points.
  • Colour needs d-d transitions (unpaired); Zn2+/Sc3+ colourless.
  • Highest states with F/O (MnO4-, CrO3); low states with pi-acceptors.
  • Interstitials (Fe3C, TiH) harden steels.
  • Spin-only mu: n=1: 1.73, 2: 2.83, 3: 3.87, 4: 4.90, 5: 5.92 BM.
Example 1.

Highest oxidation state of Cr and Mn in fluorides/oxides?

  1. CrO3/CrF6 (+6); Mn2O7/MnO4- (+7).
  2. +6 and +7.

Answer: Cr +6, Mn +7.

Chapter 12 · Topic 25

Important compounds

d- and f-Block Elementsd-f & CoordinationTopic 25 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In d- and f-Block Elements, Important compounds: KMnO4 and K2Cr2O7 are the oxidant workhorses. KMnO4 (pyrolusite fusion + CO2/electrolysis) and K2Cr2O7 (chromite fusion + acidification) oxidise by medium-set n-factors; chromate-yellow and dichromate-orange interconvert with pH.
Key formula(s).\[ Cr_2O_7^{2-}:x=6,\;2CrO_4^{2-}+2H^+\rightleftharpoons Cr_2O_7^{2-}+H_2O \]
Key points.
  • Cr2O7 2- + Fe2+ (1:6); acidified K2Cr2O7 is the primary standard.
  • Chromyl chloride test (red vapours) confirms Cl-.
  • KMnO4 attacks cold alkenes to glycols (Baeyer).
  • MnO4- + Fe2+ (1:5), + oxalate (2:5), + SO2; green MnO4 2- in alkali.
Example 1.

MnO4- oxidises SO3 2- in acid. n-factor of Mn?

  1. Mn +7 to +2.
  2. 5.

Answer: 5.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Green intermediate in alkaline MnO4- reduction?

  1. MnO4 2- manganate is green.
  2. Manganate(VI).

Answer: MnO4 2-.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using x=5 for MnO4- in alkali.
  • Calling dichromate the basic-medium species.

Key formula(s).\[ MnO_4^-:x=5/3/1\,(acid/neutral/alk),\;MnO_4^-:Fe^{2+}=1\!:\!5 \]
Key points.
  • Chromyl chloride test (red vapours) confirms Cl-.
  • KMnO4 attacks cold alkenes to glycols (Baeyer).

  • Cr2O7 2- + Fe2+ (1:6); acidified K2Cr2O7 is the primary standard.
Example 1.

KMnO4 to FeSO4 mole ratio in acid?

  1. Mn gains 5e, Fe loses 1e.
  2. 1:5.

Answer: 1:5.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Yellow chromate turns orange on adding acid. Why?

  1. Protons dimerise chromate to dichromate.
  2. pH equilibrium shift.

Answer: Chromate-dichromate equilibrium.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.

Concept. In d- and f-Block Elements, Properties of K2Cr2O7: K2Cr2O7 needs external indicator (diphenylamine). KMnO4 (pyrolusite fusion + CO2/electrolysis) and K2Cr2O7 (chromite fusion + acidification) oxidise by medium-set n-factors; chromate-yellow and dichromate-orange interconvert with pH.
Key formula(s).\[ Cr_2O_7^{2-}:x=6,\;2CrO_4^{2-}+2H^+\rightleftharpoons Cr_2O_7^{2-}+H_2O,\;MnO_4^-:Fe^{2+}=1\!:\!5,\;K_2Cr_2O_7\,primary\,standard \]
Key points.
  • Chromyl chloride test (red vapours) confirms Cl-.
  • KMnO4 attacks cold alkenes to glycols (Baeyer).
  • MnO4- + Fe2+ (1:5), + oxalate (2:5), + SO2; green MnO4 2- in alkali.
  • Cr2O7 2- + Fe2+ (1:6); acidified K2Cr2O7 is the primary standard.
Example 1.

KMnO4 to FeSO4 mole ratio in acid?

  1. Mn gains 5e, Fe loses 1e.
  2. 1:5.

Answer: 1:5.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Yellow chromate turns orange on adding acid. Why?

  1. Protons dimerise chromate to dichromate.
  2. pH equilibrium shift.

Answer: Chromate-dichromate equilibrium.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using x=5 for MnO4- in alkali.
  • Calling dichromate the basic-medium species.

Chapter 13 · Topic 1

Coordination compounds

Coordination Compoundsd-f & CoordinationTopic 1 of 45

Explanation

Concept. In Coordination Compounds, Coordination compounds: metal-ligand spheres plus counter ions define complexes. Complexes name by alphabetical ligands with Roman states, isomerise by connectivity or space, split by field geometry and stabilise by chelation.
Key formula(s).\[ CN=\\sigma\,count \]
Key points.
  • CO tops spectrochemical series.
  • EDTA titrates 1:1.
  • Werner: primary = OS, secondary = CN.
  • Cis-bis-chelate can resolve.
Example 1.

CN of Pt in [PtCl6]2-?

  1. 6 chloro ligands.
  2. 6.

Answer: 6.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Ionisation isomers test?

  1. AgNO3 precipitates free Cl-/SO4.
  2. Silver nitrate.

Answer: AgNO3 test.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Counting prefixes alphabetically.
  • Trans chirality claim.

Index / d-f & Coordination
Chapter 13 · Topic 2

Coordination entities

Coordination Compoundsd-f & CoordinationTopic 2 of 45

Explanation

Concept. In Coordination Compounds, Coordination entities: bracketed spheres carry the complex charge. Ligands donate pairs: monodentate (NH3, H2O, Cl-), bidentate (en, ox, acac), polydentate (EDTA hexadentate); chelates ring-close for stability while ambidentates (NO2-/ONO-, SCN-/NCS-) bind through either end.
Key formula(s).\[ CN=\sigma\,count,\;Werner:\,primary=OS,\,secondary=CN \]
Key points.
  • Coordination sphere [..] vs ionisation sphere outside it.
  • CN 6 octahedral and CN 4 tetrahedral/square-planar dominate.
  • Werner: primary valency = oxidation state, secondary = coordination number.
  • Chelate + macrocyclic effects multiply formation constants.
Example 1.

Denticity of EDTA and en?

  1. EDTA wraps six donor atoms.
  2. EDTA 6, en 2.

Answer: 6 and 2.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Linkage isomers of [Co(NH3)5NO2]2+?

  1. NO2- binds via N (nitro) or O (nitrito).
  2. Two isomers.

Answer: Nitro/nitrito pair.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Counting ambidentate as bidentate.
  • Putting counter ions inside the sphere.

Explanation

Key formula(s).\[ homoleptic:\,one\,ligand\,type \]

  • CN 6 octahedral and CN 4 tetrahedral/square-planar dominate.
  • Werner: primary valency = oxidation state, secondary = coordination number.
  • Chelate + macrocyclic effects multiply formation constants.
  • Coordination sphere [..] vs ionisation sphere outside it.
Example 1.

CN and oxidation state of Fe in [Fe(CN)6]4-?

  1. 6 CN- ligands: CN = 6; charge balance Fe + 6(-1) = -4.
  2. Fe = +2.

Answer: CN 6, Fe(II).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Chelate rings in [Cu(en)2]2+?

  1. Each en forms one 5-membered ring.
  2. 2 rings.

Answer: 2 chelate rings.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Counting ambidentate as bidentate.
  • Putting counter ions inside the sphere.

Answer: 6 and 2.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Linkage isomers of [Co(NH3)5NO2]2+?

  1. NO2- binds via N (nitro) or O (nitrito).
  2. Two isomers.

Answer: Nitro/nitrito pair.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Counting ambidentate as bidentate.
  • Putting counter ions inside the sphere.

Chapter 13 · Topic 17

Nomenclature of coordination compounds

Coordination Compoundsd-f & CoordinationTopic 17 of 45

Explanation

Concept. In Coordination Compounds, Nomenclature of coordination compounds: alphabetical ligands plus Roman states name complexes. Name ligands alphabetically with di/tri, metal with -ate for anionic spheres and Roman oxidation states; isomerism splits structural (ionisation, solvate, linkage, coordination) versus stereo (cis-trans/fac-mer geometric, chiral optical).
Key formula(s).\[ MA_2B_2\,(sq):\,cis+trans,\;MA_3B_3\,(oct):\,fac+mer \]
Key points.
  • [Co(NH3)5SO4]Br vs [Co(NH3)5Br]SO4: ionisation isomers (AgNO3 test).
  • [Cr(H2O)6]Cl3 violet vs [CrCl(H2O)5]Cl2 green: solvate pair.
  • Geometrical needs two identical ligands cis/trans capable.
  • Optical needs no improper rotation (cis-bis-chelate qualifies).
Example 1.

Name [Cu(NH3)4]SO4.

  1. Cation tetraamminecopper(II), anion sulphate.
  2. Tetraamminecopper(II) sulphate.

Answer: Tetraamminecopper(II) sulphate.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which is chiral: cis- or trans-[Co(en)2Cl2]+?

  1. Trans has a mirror plane; cis lacks symmetry.
  2. Cis (resolvable pair).

Answer: Cis isomer.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Alphabetising with di/tri prefixes counted.
  • Expecting optical activity from trans isomers.

Chapter 13 · Topic 26

Valence bond theory

Coordination Compoundsd-f & CoordinationTopic 26 of 45

Explanation

Concept. In Coordination Compounds, Valence bond theory: valence bond theory overlaps atomic orbitals into directional bonds. VBT sorts complexes by pairing: inner-orbital (n-1)d2sp3 low-spin with strong ligands vs outer sp3d2 high-spin with weak ligands; magnetism counts the leftovers.
Key formula(s).\[ strong\,(CN^-,CO,en)\to pairing,\;weak\,(F^-,H_2O)\to high\!-\!spin \]
Key points.
  • [Fe(CN)6]4- d2sp3 diamagnetic; [FeF6]3- sp3d2 with 5 unpaired.
  • Square planar dsp2 for Ni2+/Pd2+/Pt2+ with strong fields.
  • Tetrahedral always high-spin (small Delta-t).
  • CO is the strongest-field common ligand.
Example 1.

Hybridisation and magnetism of [Ni(CN)4]2-?

  1. Strong CN- pairs Ni2+ d8 to one hole pair... dsp2.
  2. Diamagnetic square planar.

Answer: dsp2, diamagnetic.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) [CoF6]3- inner or outer? Magnetism?

  1. F- is weak: no pairing, sp3d2.
  2. 4 unpaired, paramagnetic.

Answer: Outer orbital, 4 unpaired.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Pairing electrons for weak-field ligands.
  • Assigning tetrahedral low-spin states.

Key formula(s).\[ (n-1)d^2sp^3\,low\!-\!spin \]
Key points.
  • Square planar dsp2 for Ni2+/Pd2+/Pt2+ with strong fields.
  • Tetrahedral always high-spin (small Delta-t).
  • CO is the strongest-field common ligand.
  • [Fe(CN)6]4- d2sp3 diamagnetic; [FeF6]3- sp3d2 with 5 unpaired.
Example 1.

[Fe(CN)6]3- unpaired electrons?

  1. Strong field d5 low-spin: t2g5.
  2. 1 unpaired.

Answer: 1.

Chapter 13 · Topic 31

Crystal field theory

Coordination Compoundsd-f & CoordinationTopic 31 of 45

Explanation

Concept. In Coordination Compounds, Crystal field theory: CFT splits d-orbitals by ligand geometry. CFT splits d-orbitals (octahedral t2g-eg gap Delta-o; tetrahedral inverted gap 4/9 Delta-o; square planar extreme) with CFSE deciding high vs low spin by pairing energy; absorbed colour complements what we see.
Key formula(s).\[ series:\,CO>CN^->en>NH_3>H_2O>F^->Cl^-,\;high\,vs\,low:\,pairing\,energy\,calls \]
Key points.
  • Seen colour is complementary to absorbed (Ti3+ purple absorbs green-yellow).
  • Jahn-Teller distorts uneven eg (Cu2+ elongated).
  • d4-d7 octahedral go high-spin with weak, low-spin with strong ligands.
  • Delta grows with oxidation state and down groups (3d<4d<5d).
Example 1.

CFSE of high-spin d5 octahedral?

  1. t2g3 eg2: CFSE = 3(-0.4) + 2(0.6) = 0.
  2. Zero.

Answer: 0 Delta-o.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Strongest-field ligand among F-, H2O, NH3, CO?

  1. Spectrochemical order rises to pi-acceptors.
  2. CO.

Answer: CO.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using Delta-o for tetrahedral splitting.
  • Reporting absorbed colour as observed.

  • Delta grows with oxidation state and down groups (3d<4d<5d).

  • Jahn-Teller distorts uneven eg (Cu2+ elongated).

  2. Zero.

Explanation

Concept. In Coordination Compounds, Crystal field splitting: geometry and spectrochemical rank fix splitting size. CFT splits d-orbitals (octahedral t2g-eg gap Delta-o; tetrahedral inverted gap 4/9 Delta-o; square planar extreme) with CFSE deciding high vs low spin by pairing energy; absorbed colour complements what we see.
Key formula(s).\[ Jahn\!-\!Teller:\,Cu^{2+}\,elongates \],\;\Delta_t=\frac{4}{9}\Delta_o \]
Key points.
  • d4-d7 octahedral go high-spin with weak, low-spin with strong ligands.
  • Delta grows with oxidation state and down groups (3d<4d<5d).
  • Seen colour is complementary to absorbed (Ti3+ purple absorbs green-yellow).
  • Jahn-Teller distorts uneven eg (Cu2+ elongated).
Example 1.

CFSE of high-spin d5 octahedral?

  1. t2g3 eg2: CFSE = 3(-0.4) + 2(0.6) = 0.
  2. Zero.

Answer: 0 Delta-o.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Strongest-field ligand among F-, H2O, NH3, CO?

  1. Spectrochemical order rises to pi-acceptors.
  2. CO.

Answer: CO.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using Delta-o for tetrahedral splitting.
  • Reporting absorbed colour as observed.

  • Delta grows with oxidation state and down groups (3d<4d<5d).

  • Jahn-Teller distorts uneven eg (Cu2+ elongated).
  • d4-d7 octahedral go high-spin with weak, low-spin with strong ligands.
Example 1.

CFSE of low-spin d6 octahedral?

  1. t2g6 eg0: 6(-0.4).
  2. -2.4 Delta-o (+2P pairing).

Answer: -2.4 Delta-o.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Weakest-field ligand among NH3, H2O, F-, CO?

Chapter 13 · Topic 42

Stability of complexes

Coordination Compoundsd-f & CoordinationTopic 42 of 45

Explanation

Concept. In Coordination Compounds, Stability of complexes: Kf and chelate rings grade complex persistence. Stability constants Kf (overall beta for stepwise K1K2...) rise with chelation, small highly-charged metals and strong donors; EDTA titrations, cisplatin drugs and chlorophyll/haemoglobin all exploit tuned stability.
Key formula(s).\[ \log\beta\uparrow\,with\,chelate\,rings,\;entropy\,chelate \]
Key points.
  • 5/6-membered rings most stable.
  • EDTA complexes 1:1 (water hardness titration).
  • Ag(CN)2- leaches gold/silver ores.
  • Chelate effect is entropy-driven (many H2O freed).
Example 1.

beta3 for K1=1e4, K2=1e3, K3=1e2?

  1. beta = product of stepwise K.
  2. beta3 = 1e9.

Answer: 1e9.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why is EDTA titration 1:1?

  1. One EDTA wraps one metal fully.
  2. Hexadentate 1:1 stoichiometry.

Answer: 1:1 complex.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Attributing chelate effect to enthalpy alone.
  • Inverting Kf and Kd meanings.

Example 1.

Why is [Cu(en)2]2+ stabler than [Cu(NH3)4]2+?

  1. en chelates: two rings release four waters.
  2. Entropy-driven chelate effect.

Answer: Chelate entropy gain.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Reagent for water hardness estimation?

  1. EDTA forms 1:1 complexes with Ca2+/Mg2+.
  2. EDTA titration (Eriochrome Black T).

Answer: EDTA.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Attributing chelate effect to enthalpy alone.
  • Inverting Kf and Kd meanings.

Chapter 14 · Topic 1

Minerals and ores

Metallurgy / General Principles of ExtractionAppliedTopic 1 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Metallurgy, Minerals and ores: ores are workable mineral deposits with gangue. Ores are dressed by density (washing), magnetism, froth flotation (sulphides with pine oil/xanthate) or leaching (Au-CN, Al-bauxite Bayer); calcination (no air) and roasting (excess air) prep oxides before flux-aided smelting slags off gangue.
Key formula(s).\[ flux+gangue\to slag,\;hydraulic:\,water\,washes\,gangue \]
Key points.
  • Froth: sulphide wets oil froth, gangue sinks in water.
  • Bayer leach: Al2O3 dissolves in NaOH, Fe2O3 filtered.
  • Flux acidic (SiO2) for basic gangue and reverse.
  • Calcination of carbonates/hydrates; roasting of sulphides.
Example 1.

Method to concentrate galena (PbS)?

  1. Sulphide ore: oil-froth lifts it.
  2. Froth flotation.

Answer: Froth flotation.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Calcination vs roasting atmosphere?

  1. Calcination: absent/limited air; roasting: excess air.
  2. Air supply differs.

Answer: Limited vs excess air.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Floating oxide ores by froth.
  • Roasting carbonates (calcine them).

Index / Applied
Chapter 14 · Topic 2

Gangue

Metallurgy / General Principles of ExtractionAppliedTopic 2 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Metallurgy, Gangue: worthless gangue must be separated before smelting. Ores are dressed by density (washing), magnetism, froth flotation (sulphides with pine oil/xanthate) or leaching (Au-CN, Al-bauxite Bayer); calcination (no air) and roasting (excess air) prep oxides before flux-aided smelting slags off gangue.
Key formula(s).\[ Au+CN^-/O_2\to[Au(CN)_2]^-,\;flux+gangue\to slag,\;hydraulic:\,water\,washes\,gangue \]
Key points.
  • Bayer leach: Al2O3 dissolves in NaOH, Fe2O3 filtered.
  • Flux acidic (SiO2) for basic gangue and reverse.
  • Calcination of carbonates/hydrates; roasting of sulphides.
  • Froth: sulphide wets oil froth, gangue sinks in water.
Example 1.

Depressant in galena-sphalerite separation?

  1. NaCN films ZnS, blocking xanthate.
  2. NaCN depresses ZnS.

Answer: NaCN.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Collector and frother examples?

  1. Xanthate collects sulphides; pine oil froths.
  2. Xanthate + pine oil.

Answer: Xanthate, pine oil.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Floating oxide ores by froth.
  • Roasting carbonates (calcine them).

Chapter 14 · Topic 9

Roasting

Metallurgy / General Principles of ExtractionAppliedTopic 9 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Metallurgy, Roasting: excess-air heating converts sulphides to oxides. Ores are dressed by density (washing), magnetism, froth flotation (sulphides with pine oil/xanthate) or leaching (Au-CN, Al-bauxite Bayer); calcination (no air) and roasting (excess air) prep oxides before flux-aided smelting slags off gangue.
Key formula(s).\[ Au+CN^-/O_2\to[Au(CN)_2]^-,\;flux+gangue\to slag \]
Key points.
  • Flux acidic (SiO2) for basic gangue and reverse.
  • Calcination of carbonates/hydrates; roasting of sulphides.
  • Froth: sulphide wets oil froth, gangue sinks in water.
  • Bayer leach: Al2O3 dissolves in NaOH, Fe2O3 filtered.
Example 1.

Chief ore of Al and Fe?

  1. Bauxite Al2O3.2H2O; haematite Fe2O3.
  2. Bauxite, haematite.

Answer: Bauxite / haematite.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Flux for acidic gangue?

  1. Basic CaO/CaCO3 flux.
  2. Limestone.

Answer: Basic flux.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Floating oxide ores by froth.
  • Roasting carbonates (calcine them).

Chapter 14 · Topic 13

Reduction of metal oxides

Metallurgy / General Principles of ExtractionAppliedTopic 13 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Metallurgy, Reduction of metal oxides: carbon, hydrogen, self or electrolytic routes strip oxygen. Ellingham plots Delta-G-zero vs T: lower lines reduce higher oxides; carbon wins above ~1000 C for Fe/Zn, H2 suits Mo/W, self-reduction runs Cu/Pb sulphides, and fused electrolysis takes Al/Mg/Na.
Key formula(s).\[ self:\,Cu_2S+2Cu_2O\to6Cu \]
Key points.
  • 2C + O2 line slopes down steeply (gas moles rise).
  • Mg reduces Al2O3 only where its line dips below.
  • Self-reduction: 2Cu2S + 3O2 -> 2Cu2O + 2SO2 then Cu2S + 2Cu2O -> 6Cu.
  • Highly reactive metals need electrolysis, never carbon.
Example 1.

Can carbon reduce MgO at 1500 C?

  1. Mg/MgO line stays below C/CO at that T.
  2. No (Mg holds oxygen tighter).

Answer: No.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why is Al extracted electrolytically?

  1. Al2O3 line sits below carbon lines at all practical T.
  2. Only electrolysis (Hall-Heroult) works.

Answer: Carbon cannot reduce Al2O3.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading Ellingham slopes backwards.
  • Proposing carbon for alkali metals.

Answer: Cu2S/Cu2O couple.

Chapter 14 · Topic 20

Refining

Metallurgy / General Principles of ExtractionAppliedTopic 20 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Metallurgy, Refining: refining matches impurity chemistry to method. Refining matches impurity chemistry: distillation (Zn/Hg), liquation (Sn/Pb), electrolytic (Cu/Ag blister to cathode), zone (Ge/Si ultra-pure), vapour-phase Mond Ni(CO)4 and van Arkel ZrI4 for refractory metals.
Key formula(s).\[ zone:\,impurity\,in\,melt \]
Key points.
  • Zone refining exploits segregation coefficient < 1.
  • Mond: volatile carbonyl forms at 50 C, cracks at 230 C.
  • van Arkel: iodide decomposes on hot filament.
  • Blister copper anode slimes collect Ag/Au.
Example 1.

Carbonyl decomposition temperature for Ni?

  1. Ni(CO)4 forms ~50 C, cracks ~230 C.
  2. 230 C.

Answer: ~230 C.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Metal refined on hot tungsten filament as iodide?

  1. ZrI4 decomposes on the filament.
  2. Zr (van Arkel).

Answer: Zirconium.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using Mond for Zr (that is van Arkel).
  • Electrolysing for semiconductor-grade Si.

Chapter 14 · Topic 28

Important extraction examples

Metallurgy / General Principles of ExtractionAppliedTopic 28 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Metallurgy, Important extraction examples: Al, Fe, Cu and Zn showcase every extraction route. Al comes from Bayer alumina plus Hall-Heroult cryolite electrolysis; Fe from blast-furnace CO/coke with limestone slag; Cu by self-reduction of matte; Zn by roasting plus carbon reduction/distillation.
Key formula(s).\[ Bayer:\,Al_2O_3/NaOH,\;blast:\,Fe_2O_3+3CO\to2Fe \]
Key points.
  • Cryolite Na3AlF6 drops alumina melting to ~950 C.
  • Blast zones: combustion, reduction, slag, melting stacked vertically.
  • Copper matte (Cu2S + FeS) Bessemerises to blister Cu.
  • Zn distils off (bp 907 C) and condenses.
Example 1.

Role of cryolite in aluminium extraction?

  1. Dissolves Al2O3 and lowers melting point.
  2. Also raises conductivity.

Answer: Flux + conductivity + lower mp.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Slag in iron extraction?

Chapter 14 · Topic 29

Aluminium extraction

Metallurgy / General Principles of ExtractionAppliedTopic 29 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Metallurgy, Aluminium extraction: Bayer plus Hall-Heroult cryolite electrolysis make Al. Al comes from Bayer alumina plus Hall-Heroult cryolite electrolysis; Fe from blast-furnace CO/coke with limestone slag; Cu by self-reduction of matte; Zn by roasting plus carbon reduction/distillation.
Key formula(s).\[ Bayer:\,Al_2O_3/NaOH,\;cryolite\,fluxes\,alumina \]
Key points.
  • Blast zones: combustion, reduction, slag, melting stacked vertically.
  • Copper matte (Cu2S + FeS) Bessemerises to blister Cu.
  • Zn distils off (bp 907 C) and condenses.
  • Cryolite Na3AlF6 drops alumina melting to ~950 C.
Example 1.

Cathode/anode products in Hall-Heroult?

  1. Al3+ discharges at cathode; carbon anode burns to CO/CO2.
  2. Al metal + carbon oxides.

Answer: Al at cathode.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Iron oxide reduced first in blast furnace?

  1. Indirect CO reduction starts near the top.
  2. Fe2O3 by CO.

Answer: CO reduces Fe2O3.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling cryolite the ore (bauxite is).
  • Missing limestone as flux source.

Chapter 15 · Topic 1

Preliminary tests

Qualitative Inorganic AnalysisAppliedTopic 1 of 47

Explanation

Concept. In Qualitative Inorganic Analysis, Preliminary tests: dry and wet screens shortlist ions fast. Dry tests screen fast: flame colours (Na golden, K lilac, Ca brick, Ba green, Cu blue-green), charcoal cavity reductions, and borax-bead metaborate colours (Cu blue-green hot, Co deep blue, Fe yellow-brown, Cr green).
Key formula(s).\[ blue\,glass\,for\,K,\;solubility\,pre\!-\!sorts \]
Key points.
  • Charcoal cavity: ZnO yellow-hot incrustation, Pb grey beads.
  • Flame through blue glass unmasks K from Na.
  • Solubility groups (HCl, H2SO4...) pre-sort anions.
  • Borax bead oxidising vs reducing flames can differ (Cu blue vs red opaque).
Example 1.

Apple-green flame indicates?

  1. Ba2+ volatile chloride paints green.
  2. Barium.

Answer: Ba2+.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Blue-green copper flame masked by what?

  1. Nothing masks Cu strongly; K needs blue glass vs Na.
  2. Blue glass is for K/Na pair.

Answer: Blue glass for K.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading bead colours in the wrong flame.
  • Skipping the blue-glass check for K.
Back to Index
Index / Applied
Chapter 15 · Topic 2

Dry tests

Qualitative Inorganic AnalysisAppliedTopic 2 of 47

Explanation

Concept. In Qualitative Inorganic Analysis, Dry tests: flame, bead and cavity tests need no solution. Dry tests screen fast: flame colours (Na golden, K lilac, Ca brick, Ba green, Cu blue-green), charcoal cavity reductions, and borax-bead metaborate colours (Cu blue-green hot, Co deep blue, Fe yellow-brown, Cr green).
Key formula(s).\[ bead:\,Na_2B_4O_7\to2NaBO_2+B_2O_3,\;oxide\,colours\,in\,bead \]
Key points.
  • Flame through blue glass unmasks K from Na.
  • Solubility groups (HCl, H2SO4...) pre-sort anions.
  • Borax bead oxidising vs reducing flames can differ (Cu blue vs red opaque).
  • Charcoal cavity: ZnO yellow-hot incrustation, Pb grey beads.
Example 1.

Blue bead in oxidising flame suggests?

  1. Cu gives transparent blue-green hot bead.
  2. Copper (Co gives deeper pure blue).

Answer: Copper.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Yellow-hot, white-cold incrustation on charcoal?

  1. Classic ZnO behaviour.
  2. Zinc.

Answer: Zn.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading bead colours in the wrong flame.
  • Skipping the blue-glass check for K.

Chapter 15 · Topic 9

Group separation of cations

Qualitative Inorganic AnalysisAppliedTopic 9 of 47

Explanation

Concept. In Qualitative Inorganic Analysis, Group separation of cations: staged reagents drop cation groups I to VI. Cations fall by staged reagents: I (dil HCl: Ag+, Pb2+, Hg2 2+ chlorides), II (H2S in acid), III (NH4Cl + NH4OH hydroxides), IV (H2S in base), V ((NH4)2CO3 carbonates), VI (Mg2+ + rest); phosphate/oxalate/borate must be removed first.
Key formula(s).\[ S^{2-}\,tiny\,in\,acid,\;phosphate\,must\,go\,first \]
Key points.
  • NH4Cl buffers OH- so only Group III hydroxides (low Ksp) fall.
  • Acid in Group II keeps S2- tiny for selective sulphides.
  • Oxalate/phosphate precipitate Group III early - expel by ignition + HNO3.
  • Mg2+ confirmed only after Group V removal.
Example 1.

Why is NH4Cl added before NH4OH in Group III?

  1. Common ion clamps OH- low.
  2. Only III hydroxides exceed Ksp; IV/V stay dissolved.

Answer: Selective low OH- precipitation.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Group II reagent and medium?

  1. H2S in dilute HCl.
  2. Acidic sulphide precipitation.

Answer: H2S / H+.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Passing H2S without acid control (wrong groups fall).
  • Forgetting to expel phosphate first.
Back to Index
Index / Applied

Group I cations

Qualitative Inorganic AnalysisAppliedTopic 10 of 47

Explanation

Cations fall by staged reagents: I (dil HCl: Ag+, Pb2+, Hg2 2+ chlorides), II (H2S in acid), III (NH4Cl + NH4OH hydroxides), IV (H2S in base), V ((NH4)2CO3 carbonates), VI (Mg2+ + rest); phosphate/oxalate/borate must be removed first.
Key formula(s).\[ I:HCl,\;II:H_2S/H^+ \]
Key points.
  • Acid in Group II keeps S2- tiny for selective sulphides.
  • Oxalate/phosphate precipitate Group III early - expel by ignition + HNO3.
  • Mg2+ confirmed only after Group V removal.
  • NH4Cl buffers OH- so only Group III hydroxides (low Ksp) fall.
Example 1.

Why does Pb2+ appear in both Group I and II?

  1. PbCl2 partly soluble: residue falls in II as PbS.
  2. Split precipitation.

Answer: Partial chloride solubility.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Group V reagent?

  1. (NH4)2CO3 in ammonia.
  2. Carbonates of Ba/Sr/Ca.

Answer: (NH4)2CO3.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Passing H2S without acid control (wrong groups fall).

Each cation has a fingerprint: NH4+ (Nessler brown), Pb2+ (yellow PbI2/CrO4), Cu2+ (deep-blue ammine), Fe3+ (blood-red thiocyanate, Prussian blue), Ni2+ (red DMG), Co2+ (blue thiocyanate), Zn2+ (white ferrocyanide), Mn2+ (violet fusion), flame colours for Ba/Sr/Ca.
Key formula(s).\[ Mg^{2+}:\,magneson\,blue \],\;Fe^{3+}+SCN^-\to blood\!-\!red \]
Key points.
  • Fe2+ gives dark-blue Turnbull with ferricyanide; Fe3+ Prussian blue with ferrocyanide.
  • Al3+ lake test with litmus/aluminon; Cr3+ yellow chromate after fusion.
  • Ba green, Sr crimson, Ca brick-red flames.
  • PbCl2 re-dissolves hot (Group I trick).
Example 1.

White fumes with HCl rod indicate which ion?

  1. NH3 + HCl -> NH4Cl white fumes.
  2. NH4+.

Answer: NH4+.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Pb2+ vs Ag+ both give white chlorides. Distinguish?

  1. PbCl2 dissolves in hot water, AgCl does not.
  2. Hot-water solubility test.

Answer: PbCl2 hot-soluble.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.

  • Calling Sr flame brick-red (that is Ca).

Anions answer dilute/conc H2SO4 plus specific tests: carbonates fizz CO2 (limewater milky), Cl-/Br-/I- give AgX colours and chromyl (Cl only), NO3- rings brown, SO4 2- BaSO4 insoluble in acid, acetate smells vinegar with H2SO4.
Key formula(s).\[ ring:\,[Fe(H_2O)_5NO]^{2+},\;sulphite:\,SO_2\,smell \]
Key points.
  • Brown ring needs fresh FeSO4 layered under conc H2SO4.
  • BaSO4 survives HCl; BaSO3/BaCO3 dissolve.
  • Borate + HF... ethyl borate burns green-edged.
  • Chromyl chloride (red vapours) is Cl--only proof.
Example 1.

Limewater turns milky then clears. Ion?

  1. CO2 milks limewater; excess dissolves as bicarbonate.
  2. CO3 2- (or HCO3-).

Answer: Carbonate.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Red vapours with K2Cr2O7 + conc H2SO4?

  1. Chromyl chloride forms only from Cl-.
  2. Chloride.

Answer: Cl-.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Trusting any white silver precipitate as Cl- (check solubility).
  • Using old FeSO4 for the ring test.

Chapter 15 · Topic 47

Interference and group separation

Qualitative Inorganic AnalysisAppliedTopic 47 of 47

Explanation

Concept. In Qualitative Inorganic Analysis, Interference and group separation: phosphate/oxalate/borate must be expelled first. Cations fall by staged reagents: I (dil HCl: Ag+, Pb2+, Hg2 2+ chlorides), II (H2S in acid), III (NH4Cl + NH4OH hydroxides), IV (H2S in base), V ((NH4)2CO3 carbonates), VI (Mg2+ + rest); phosphate/oxalate/borate must be removed first.
Key formula(s).\[ phosphate\,must\,go\,first \]
Key points.
  • Oxalate/phosphate precipitate Group III early - expel by ignition + HNO3.
  • Mg2+ confirmed only after Group V removal.
  • NH4Cl buffers OH- so only Group III hydroxides (low Ksp) fall.
  • Acid in Group II keeps S2- tiny for selective sulphides.
Example 1.

Why is NH4Cl added before NH4OH in Group III?

  1. Common ion clamps OH- low.
  2. Only III hydroxides exceed Ksp; IV/V stay dissolved.

Answer: Selective low OH- precipitation.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Group II reagent and medium?

  1. H2S in dilute HCl.
  2. Acidic sulphide precipitation.

Answer: H2S / H+.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Passing H2S without acid control (wrong groups fall).
  • Forgetting to expel phosphate first.

Chapter 16 · Topic 1

Air pollution

Environmental ChemistryAppliedTopic 1 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Environmental Chemistry, Air pollution: primary emissions react into secondary smog and acid rain. Primary pollutants (CO, SO2, NOx, particulates) react into secondary smog (O3, PAN) and acid rain (H2SO4/HNO3, pH<5.6); CO2/CH4 greenhouse-trap IR while CFC chlorine cycles shred stratospheric ozone.
Key formula(s).\[ smog:\,NO_x+VOC+h\\nu\to O_3+PAN,\;acid\,rain\,pH<5.6 \]
Key points.
  • Limestone/marble cancer: CaCO3 + acid -> soluble salts.
  • Montreal Protocol froze CFCs.
  • CO binds haemoglobin (carboxy, ~250x affinity).
  • Photochemical smog peaks at noon (oxidants); London smog was reductive soot.
Example 1.

Classical vs photochemical smog difference?

  1. London: soot + SO2, reducing, winter mornings.
  2. LA: NOx + VOC + sun, oxidising, noon.

Answer: Reductive vs oxidative smog.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Stone leprosy on marble is caused by?

  1. Acid rain converts CaCO3 to soluble CaSO4/Ca(NO3)2.
  2. SO2/NOx-derived acids.

Answer: Acid rain.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling CO2 the smog oxidant (it is O3/PAN).
  • Mixing ozone-layer healing with warming.

Chapter 16 · Topic 15

Water pollution

Environmental ChemistryAppliedTopic 15 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Environmental Chemistry, Water pollution: oxygen-ledger BOD/COD grades water filth. Water quality runs on oxygen ledger: BOD (5-day microbial demand) and COD (dichromate total) rise with sewage/effluents; phosphates trigger algal eutrophication; green chemistry answers with atom economy, catalysis and benign solvents.
Key formula(s).\[ BOD\,(mg/L)\uparrow\,=\,dirtier,\;COD\ge BOD \]
Key points.
  • COD uses K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 oxidation of everything oxidisable.
  • Eutrophication ends in hypoxic dead zones.
  • Soil pollutants: pesticides, heavy metals, e-waste leachates.
  • Clean water BOD < 5 ppm; sewage > 17 ppm.
Example 1.

COD vs BOD relation?

  1. Dichromate oxidises more than microbes.
  2. COD > BOD always.

Answer: COD higher.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Green chemistry principle example?

  1. Catalytic routes cut waste (atom economy).
  2. Catalysis over stoichiometric reagents.

Answer: Catalysis.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Expecting BOD above COD (COD always higher).
  • Blaming nitrates alone for eutrophication (phosphates lead).

Chapter 17 · Topic 1

Stoichiometry in metallurgy

Metallurgy & Inorganic Numerical ConceptsMasteryTopic 1 of 12

Explanation

Concept. In Metallurgy and Inorganic Numerical Concepts, Stoichiometry in metallurgy: ore-to-metal math runs on balanced roasting/reduction equations. Metallurgical numbers price ore purity, Ellingham feasibility and electrolytic metal per coulomb.
Key formula(s).\[ \\Delta G<0\,feasible,\;w=MIt/nF \]
Key points.
  • Grade = pure over sample.
  • Crossing T flips reducer.
  • Series cells share charge.
  • Slag mass balances.
Example 1.

Ore 80% pure, 100 kg: metal at 90% recovery (metal 70% of pure)?

  1. Pure 80 kg; metal 56 kg; recovered 50.4 kg.
  2. 50.4 kg.

Answer: 50.4 kg.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) 96500 C deposits how much Al (n=3, M=27)?

  1. Moles e = 1; Al = 1/3 mol = 9 g.
  2. 9 g.

Answer: 9 g.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Grade-yield mixing.
  • n missed in Faraday.

Chapter 17 · Topic 2

Percentage purity of ores

Metallurgy & Inorganic Numerical ConceptsMasteryTopic 2 of 12

Explanation

Concept. In Metallurgy and Inorganic Numerical Concepts, Percentage purity of ores: pure mass over sample mass fixes ore grade. Metallurgical numbers price ore purity, Ellingham feasibility and electrolytic metal per coulomb.
Key formula(s).\[ %recovery=mass\,ratios \]
Key points.
  • Crossing T flips reducer.
  • Series cells share charge.
  • Slag mass balances.
  • Grade = pure over sample.
Example 1.

Bauxite 60% Al2O3, 1000 kg ore: max Al metal? At 85% recovery?

  1. Al2O3 = 600 kg; Al share = 54/102.
  2. Max = 317.6 kg; recovered = 270 kg.

Answer: 270 kg.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) 9650 C through series AgNO3 + CuSO4 cells: masses?

  1. e- = 0.1 mol: Ag = 10.8 g, Cu = 0.05 mol = 3.175 g.
  2. Same charge, M/n scaling.

Answer: 10.8 g Ag, 3.175 g Cu.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Grade-yield mixing.
  • n missed in Faraday.

Chapter 17 · Topic 9

Ellingham-diagram problems

Metallurgy & Inorganic Numerical ConceptsMasteryTopic 9 of 12

Explanation

Concept. In Metallurgy and Inorganic Numerical Concepts, Ellingham-diagram problems: line crossings pick feasible reducer-temperature pairs. Ellingham plots Delta-G-zero vs T: lower lines reduce higher oxides; carbon wins above ~1000 C for Fe/Zn, H2 suits Mo/W, self-reduction runs Cu/Pb sulphides, and fused electrolysis takes Al/Mg/Na.
Key formula(s).\[ \Delta G<0\,spontaneous,\;crossing\,T\,flips\,reducer \]
Key points.
  • Self-reduction: 2Cu2S + 3O2 -> 2Cu2O + 2SO2 then Cu2S + 2Cu2O -> 6Cu.
  • Highly reactive metals need electrolysis, never carbon.
  • 2C + O2 line slopes down steeply (gas moles rise).
  • Mg reduces Al2O3 only where its line dips below.
Example 1.

Can carbon reduce MgO at 1500 C?

  1. Mg/MgO line stays below C/CO at that T.
  2. No (Mg holds oxygen tighter).

Answer: No.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why is Al extracted electrolytically?

  1. Al2O3 line sits below carbon lines at all practical T.
  2. Only electrolysis (Hall-Heroult) works.

Answer: Carbon cannot reduce Al2O3.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading Ellingham slopes backwards.
  • Proposing carbon for alkali metals.

Index / Mastery

Chapter 18 · Topic 1

Acid-base reactions

Inorganic Reaction & Conversion Master ChapterMasteryTopic 1 of 16

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Reaction and Conversion Master, Acid-base reactions: proton transfers flag acid-base steps in mixtures. Conversion chains are cracked by OS ladders first, then colour and gas clues pick reagents and products step by step.
Key formula(s).\[ H^+ + OH^- \to H_2O \]
Key points.
  • Yellow ppt = PbI2/PbCrO4.
  • Deep blue = Cu ammine.
  • Blood red = Fe-SCN.
  • Brown gas = NO2.
Example 1.

Green solution + NaOH gives green ppt turning brown in air: ion?

  1. Green ppt = Fe(OH)2 oxidising to brown Fe(OH)3.
  2. Fe2+.

Answer: Fe2+.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) White salt + dil H2SO4 gives gas milking limewater: anion?

  1. CO2 from carbonate.
  2. CO3 2-.

Answer: Carbonate.

Chapter 18 · Topic 10

Interconversion of oxidation states

Inorganic Reaction & Conversion Master ChapterMasteryTopic 10 of 16

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Reaction and Conversion Master, Interconversion of oxidation states: oxidant/reductant choice steers OS interconversion. Metallic character (electropositive, basic oxides, reducing) rises down and left; non-metallic rises up and right. Periodicity repeats because valence shells repeat; blocks s/p/d/f follow the filling subshell.
Key formula(s).\[ MnO_4^- \xrightarrow{+5e^-} Mn^{2+}\,(acid) \]
Key points.
  • Valency for s/p = group number or 8 minus it.
  • Period number = principal quantum number of valence shell.
  • Long form fixes Mendeleev anomalies (Ar-K, Co-Ni, Te-I) by atomic number.
  • Oxides: basic (metals) to amphoteric to acidic (non-metals) across a period.
Example 1.

Most non-metallic: Si, P, S, Cl?

  1. Rises right across the period.
  2. Cl.

Answer: Cl.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Amphoteric oxides among Na2O, Al2O3, SO2?

  1. Middle-period oxide reacts both ways.
  2. Al2O3.

Answer: Al2O3.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling Al2O3 purely basic.
  • Mixing period number with group number.

Key points.

White solid heats to brown gas + residue: guess?

(JEE pattern) Blue solution + KI gives brown: ion?

Chapter 19 · Topic 1

Lewis structures

Inorganic Structures & Geometry Master ChapterMasteryTopic 1 of 18

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Structures and Geometry Master, Lewis structures: Lewis dots complete octets around the least-electronegative centre. Lewis structures distribute valence electrons to complete octets; formal charge (valence minus assigned) picks the best skeleton, and resonance averages equivalent forms into fractional bond orders.
Key formula(s).\[ FC = V-(N+\frac{B}{2}),\;best\,form:\,min|FC|,\,negative\,on\,EN\,atom \]
Key points.
  • Formal charges nearest zero win; like charges stay apart.
  • Draw skeleton = least EN atom central (H never central).
  • Octet exceptions: electron-deficient (BeCl2, BF3), expanded (PCl5, SF6), odd-electron (NO, ClO2).
  • Resonance energy stabilises benzene, carbonate, ozone beyond any single form.
Example 1.

Formal charges in O3 (central O bonded to both, one double bond)?

  1. Central O: 6-(2+3) = +1; double-bonded O: 0; single O: -1.
  2. Sum = 0 (neutral molecule).

Answer: +1, 0, -1.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Bond order of carbonate ion?

  1. Three equivalent C-O links share one double bond over 3 positions.
  2. Order = 4/3 per bond.

Answer: 1.33.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting expanded octets need period-3+ central atoms.
  • Picking resonance forms with large charge separation.

Chapter 19 · Topic 4

VSEPR theory

Inorganic Structures & Geometry Master ChapterMasteryTopic 4 of 18

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Structures and Geometry Master, VSEPR theory: VSEPR minimises electron-domain repulsion in fixed steric shapes. VSEPR arranges electron domains to minimise repulsion (lone-lone > lone-bond > bond-bond); steric number fixes electron geometry while lone pairs carve the observed molecular shape.
Key formula(s).\[ SN = \sigma + LP,\;shapes:\,2\,linear,\,3\,trigonal,\,4\,tetrahedral,\,5\,TBP,\,6\,octahedral \]
Key points.
  • 6-domain: XeF4 square planar (2 lone pairs opposite).
  • Multiple bonds squeeze angles slightly (O=C=O stays 180).
  • AX3E is pyramidal (NH3), AX2E2 bent (H2O), AX2E linear-ish bent (SO2).
  • 5-domain: lone pairs sit equatorial (SF4 see-saw, ClF3 T-shape, XeF2 linear).
Example 1.

Shape of SF4?

  1. S has 4 bonds + 1 lone pair: SN 5, lone pair equatorial.
  2. See-saw.

Answer: See-saw.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why is H2O bent but CO2 linear?

  1. H2O oxygen carries 2 lone pairs bending the H-O-H to 104.5.
  2. CO2 carbon has zero lone pairs: linear 180.

Answer: Lone pairs on O bend water.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reporting electron geometry instead of molecular shape.
  • Putting lone pairs axial in TBP systems.

Shape of ClF3 vs XeF2?

  1. ClF3 T-shape (2 lone pairs); XeF2 linear (3 lone pairs).
  2. T vs linear.

Answer: T-shaped and linear.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Bond angle order CH4/NH3/H2O?

  1. Lone pairs squeeze: 109.5 > 107 > 104.5.
  2. CH4 > NH3 > H2O.

Answer: Descending with lone pairs.

Chapter 19 · Topic 7

Hybridisation

Inorganic Structures & Geometry Master ChapterMasteryTopic 7 of 18

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Structures and Geometry Master, Hybridisation: hybridisation mixes s/p/d into directional bonding orbitals. Hybridisation mixes s/p/d into directional orbitals: sp linear, sp2 trigonal, sp3 tetrahedral, sp3d trigonal-bipyramidal, sp3d2 octahedral; lone pairs occupy hybrids and compress angles.
Key formula(s).\[ steric\,no.\,2\to sp,\;3\to sp^2 \]
Key points.
  • Hypervalent (sp3d/d2) needs period-3+ centres.
  • dsp2 square planar appears for Ni2+/Pt2+ with strong ligands.
  • Count sigma bonds + lone pairs on the central atom for the steric number.
  • s-character shortens and strengthens bonds (sp > sp2 > sp3 in EN).
Example 1.

Hybridisation of S in SF6 and geometry?

  1. 6 sigma bonds, no lone pairs: steric 6.
  2. sp3d2, octahedral.

Answer: sp3d2 octahedral.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Hybridisation of N in NH3 vs NH4+?

  1. NH3: 3 sigma + 1 lone pair = sp3 (pyramidal).
  2. NH4+: 4 sigma = sp3 (tetrahedral).

Answer: Both sp3; shapes differ.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Counting pi bonds in the steric number.
  • Assigning sp3d to second-period centres.

Chapter 19 · Topic 9

Bond angles

Inorganic Structures & Geometry Master ChapterMasteryTopic 9 of 18

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Structures and Geometry Master, Bond angles: multiple bonds and lone pairs squeeze angles off ideal values. Bond length shortens with higher order and smaller atoms; bond angle follows repulsion hierarchy; bond enthalpy is the homolytic price per mole; bond order (MOT: half the bonding-minus-antibonding count) sets length, energy and magnetism together.
Key formula(s).\[ order=\frac{N_b-N_a}{2},\;lone\,pairs\,squeeze \]
Key points.
  • Fractional orders from resonance (CO3 2- : 1.33).
  • Angle shrinks as lone pairs grow (CH4 109.5 to NH3 107 to H2O 104.5).
  • Shorter bonds vibrate at higher IR frequency.
  • Orders: H2 1, O2 2, N2 3, CO 3 (dative-assisted triple).
Example 1.

Bond order of O2+ and its magnetism?

  1. O2 has 12 valence... order 2; removing an antibonding electron gives 2.5.
  2. One unpaired electron: paramagnetic.

Answer: 2.5, paramagnetic.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Longest bond among N2, O2, F2?

  1. Orders 3, 2, 1 respectively.
  2. F2 (single) longest.

Answer: F2.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Counting non-bonding electrons in MOT order.
  • Assuming equal orders mean equal lengths across periods.

Chapter 19 · Topic 10

Molecular polarity

Inorganic Structures & Geometry Master ChapterMasteryTopic 10 of 18

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Structures and Geometry Master, Molecular polarity: net dipole survives only in unsymmetric geometries. Dipole moment (charge times distance, in debye) vectors add over a molecule; percent ionic character benchmarks against the fully-ionic e-d value, and net zero marks non-polar geometry.
Key formula(s).\[ \%\ ionic = \frac{\mu_{obs}}{\mu_{ionic}}\times100,\;symmetric\,cancels \]
Key points.
  • Lone pairs contribute (NH3 1.47 D vs NF3 0.24 D).
  • mu = 0 is the fastest polarity test in MCQs.
  • Symmetric geometries (CO2, BF3, CCl4, PF5) cancel to zero.
  • Charge separation grows with EN gap and bond length.
Example 1.

Dipole moment of CO2 vs SO2?

  1. CO2 is linear: vectors cancel exactly.
  2. SO2 is bent with a lone pair: net mu. So 0 vs non-zero.

Answer: CO2 zero, SO2 polar.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) HCl has mu 1.08 D, bond length 127 pm. Find percent ionic character.

  1. mu-ionic = e.d = (1.602e-19)(1.27e-10) = 2.03e-29 C m = 6.1 D.
  2. % = 1.08/6.1 x 100 = 17.7%.

Answer: About 18%.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Judging polarity from bonds alone, ignoring geometry.
  • Unit slips between debye and coulomb-metre.

Chapter 19 · Topic 12

Molecular orbital diagrams

Inorganic Structures & Geometry Master ChapterMasteryTopic 12 of 18

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Structures and Geometry Master, Molecular orbital diagrams: MO ladders predict order, length and magnetism together. MOT builds orbitals by LCAO: below-14-electron diatomics order sigma-2s < pi-2p < sigma-2pz; bond order half the bonding-antibonding gap decides existence, length and magnetism.
Key formula(s).\[ CO\equiv N_2\,(BO3) \]
Key points.
  • Heteronuclear MOs skew toward the more EN atom.
  • CO is isoelectronic with N2 (BO 3).
  • He2 (BO 0) does not exist.
  • B2 (1 unpaired pair... 2 unpaired), C2 diamagnetic-ish (2 pi pairs), O2 two unpaired (paramagnetic proof).
Example 1.

Which is paramagnetic: B2, C2, N2?

  1. B2 has 2 unpaired pi electrons; C2 pairs its 4 pi electrons; N2 fully paired.
  2. B2 only.

Answer: B2.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Bond order of NO and NO+?

  1. NO (11 valence... 5 bonding over antibonding excess): BO 2.5; NO+ loses antibonding: 3.0.
  2. 2.5 and 3.0.

Answer: 2.5, 3.0.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using the wrong MO order for sub-14-electron species.
  • Forgetting heteronuclear skew.

Chapter 19 · Topic 17

Coordination number

Inorganic Structures & Geometry Master ChapterMasteryTopic 17 of 18

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Structures and Geometry Master, Coordination number: secondary valency counts sigma bonds to the metal. Ligands donate pairs: monodentate (NH3, H2O, Cl-), bidentate (en, ox, acac), polydentate (EDTA hexadentate); chelates ring-close for stability while ambidentates (NO2-/ONO-, SCN-/NCS-) bind through either end.
Key formula(s).\[ CN=\sigma\,count,\;Werner:\,primary=OS,\,secondary=CN \]
Key points.
  • Coordination sphere [..] vs ionisation sphere outside it.
  • CN 6 octahedral and CN 4 tetrahedral/square-planar dominate.
  • Werner: primary valency = oxidation state, secondary = coordination number.
  • Chelate + macrocyclic effects multiply formation constants.
Example 1.

Denticity of EDTA and en?

  1. EDTA wraps six donor atoms.
  2. EDTA 6, en 2.

Answer: 6 and 2.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Linkage isomers of [Co(NH3)5NO2]2+?

  1. NO2- binds via N (nitro) or O (nitrito).
  2. Two isomers.

Answer: Nitro/nitrito pair.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Counting ambidentate as bidentate.
  • Putting counter ions inside the sphere.

Chapter 20 · Topic 1

Anomalous behaviour

Inorganic Exceptions, Trends & Advanced Master ChapterMasteryTopic 1 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Exceptions, Trends and Advanced Master, Anomalous behaviour: first-row exceptions cluster size, EN and d-orbital gaps. First-period elements (small, no d-orbitals, high EN) behave oddly; diagonal pairs Li-Mg and Be-Al resemble from similar charge/radius. Penetration s>p>d>f leaves d/f shielding poor, so Slater Zeff rises and lanthanides contract.
Key formula(s).\[ 1st\,row:\,no\,d,\,max\,cov.\,4 \]
Key points.
  • Li-Mg and Be-Al diagonals share carbonates, nitrides, solubility habits.
  • Slater: same-shell electrons shield 0.35 (1s: 0.30); inner shells ~0.85-1.0.
  • Inert pair: heavy p-block keeps ns2 unshared (Pb2+, Bi3+ stable).
  • Lanthanide contraction makes Zr/Hf and Nb/Ta near-twins.
Example 1.

Using Slater rules, estimate Zeff for a 3s electron of Mg (Z=12, config 1s2 2s2p8 3s2).

  1. S = 8(1.0) + 2(0.35)... inner 1s,2s2p: 2(1.0)+8(0.85)+1(0.35) = 9.15.
  2. Zeff = 12-9.15 = 2.85.

Answer: About 2.85.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why are Zr and Hf chemically twins?

  1. Lanthanide contraction cancels the expected size jump.
  2. Nearly identical radii and chemistry.

Answer: Lanthanide contraction.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying Slater 0.35 to 1s electrons (use 0.30).
  • Blaming inert pair for light elements.

Chapter 20 · Topic 3

Inert pair effect

Inorganic Exceptions, Trends & Advanced Master ChapterMasteryTopic 3 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Exceptions, Trends and Advanced Master, Inert pair effect: heavy p-blockers hoard ns2, stabilising lower oxidation states. First-period elements (small, no d-orbitals, high EN) behave oddly; diagonal pairs Li-Mg and Be-Al resemble from similar charge/radius. Penetration s>p>d>f leaves d/f shielding poor, so Slater Zeff rises and lanthanides contract.

Key points.
  • Inert pair: heavy p-block keeps ns2 unshared (Pb2+, Bi3+ stable).
  • Lanthanide contraction makes Zr/Hf and Nb/Ta near-twins.
  • Li-Mg and Be-Al diagonals share carbonates, nitrides, solubility habits.
  • Slater: same-shell electrons shield 0.35 (1s: 0.30); inner shells ~0.85-1.0.
Example 1.

Using Slater rules, estimate Zeff for a 3s electron of Mg (Z=12, config 1s2 2s2p8 3s2).

  1. S = 8(1.0) + 2(0.35)... inner 1s,2s2p: 2(1.0)+8(0.85)+1(0.35) = 9.15.
  2. Zeff = 12-9.15 = 2.85.

Answer: About 2.85.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why are Zr and Hf chemically twins?

  1. Lanthanide contraction cancels the expected size jump.
  2. Nearly identical radii and chemistry.

Answer: Lanthanide contraction.

  • Applying Slater 0.35 to 1s electrons (use 0.30).

Inorganic Exceptions, Trends & Advanced Master ChapterMasteryTopic 4 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Exceptions, Trends and Advanced Master, Lanthanide contraction: poor 4f shielding shrinks lanthanides ~15 pm across. Oxidation-state stability

Inorganic Exceptions, Trends & Advanced Master ChapterMasteryTopic 5 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Exceptions, Trends and Advanced Master, Oxidation-state stability: inert pair and half/full shells anchor stable states. Master problems hunt the exception first, justify trends with Zeff/size/inert-pair logic and judge each statement alone.
Key formula(s).\[ half/full\,shells\,anchor\,states \]
Key points.
  • Contraction twins Zr/Hf.
  • Stability needs lattice/hydration/CFSE sums.
  • Match columns by elimination.
  • First-row and heavy-p exceptions dominate.
Example 1.

Higher decomposition T: MgCO3 or BaCO3?

  1. Bigger cation stabilises.
  2. BaCO3.

Answer: BaCO3.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(Match) Na-golden, K-lilac, Ca-brick, Ba-green: true set?

  1. Standard flame panel matches all four.
  2. All correct.

Answer: All match.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.

Chapter 20 · Topic 10

Lattice enthalpy trends

Inorganic Exceptions, Trends & Advanced Master ChapterMasteryTopic 10 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Exceptions, Trends and Advanced Master, Lattice enthalpy trends: charge product over distance orders lattice energy. Ionic lattices are priced by lattice enthalpy (Born-Lande: rises with charge, falls with distance) and dissected by Born-Haber cycles; Fajan rules say small/highly-charged cations and large anions push bonds covalent.
Key formula(s).\[ U \propto Z^+Z^-/r_0 \]
Key points.
  • Born-Haber: sublimation + IE + dissociation + EA + U = formation enthalpy.
  • Fajan order e.g. NaCl < MgCl2 < AlCl3 in covalence.
  • Coordinate bond: one-sided sharing (NH4+, [Fe(CN)6]4-, O3 terminal).
  • High lattice U means hard, high-melting salts (MgO > NaCl).
Example 1.

Highest lattice enthalpy among NaCl, MgO, CaO?

  1. Charge product: MgO and CaO are 2x2; Mg2+ is smaller than Ca2+.
  2. MgO wins.

Answer: MgO.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Arrange NaCl, MgCl2, AlCl3 by melting point.

  1. Covalent character rises with cation charge (Fajan).
  2. NaCl > MgCl2 > AlCl3 (sublimes).

Answer: NaCl highest, AlCl3 lowest.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using only size and ignoring charge products.
  • Calling coordinate bonds purely ionic.

Chapter 20 · Topic 15

Magnetic behaviour

Inorganic Exceptions, Trends & Advanced Master ChapterMasteryTopic 15 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Inorganic Exceptions, Trends and Advanced Master, Magnetic behaviour: unpaired MO electrons make bulk paramagnetism. MOT builds orbitals by LCAO: below-14-electron diatomics order sigma-2s < pi-2p < sigma-2pz; bond order half the bonding-antibonding gap decides existence, length and magnetism.
Key formula(s).\[ \mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)} \]
Key points.
  • CO is isoelectronic with N2 (BO 3).
  • He2 (BO 0) does not exist.
  • B2 (1 unpaired pair... 2 unpaired), C2 diamagnetic-ish (2 pi pairs), O2 two unpaired (paramagnetic proof).
  • Heteronuclear MOs skew toward the more EN atom.
Example 1.

Which is paramagnetic: B2, C2, N2?

  1. B2 has 2 unpaired pi electrons; C2 pairs its 4 pi electrons; N2 fully paired.
  2. B2 only.

Answer: B2.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Bond order of NO and NO+?

  1. NO (11 valence... 5 bonding over antibonding excess): BO 2.5; NO+ loses antibonding: 3.0.
  2. 2.5 and 3.0.

Answer: 2.5, 3.0.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using the wrong MO order for sub-14-electron species.
  • Forgetting heteronuclear skew.
